members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

events.name: helix-change

events.description: Fired when the panel opens.
events.name: helix-open

attributes.name: appearance
attributes.description:
Whether the field is a text box with a swatch on it, or only the swatch.

`swatch` is the native control's shape: a block of color that opens a
picker, with no text beside it. It is what a toolbar wants, and a form that
asks for a color among twenty other questions, where a hex in a box is
eleven characters of noise next to the thing itself.

It also settles where the value is stated. The default field *is* the input,
so the panel is told `no-value` and would otherwise show a second one. A
swatch states nothing, so the panel keeps its own row and the value is
readable and typeable exactly once, in whichever of the two is present.

The trade is real and is the reason this is not the default: a swatch cannot
be read or pasted into without opening the panel, which is worse for a form
where the color is the answer rather than a setting.

attributes.name: alpha
attributes.description: Whether the color carries an alpha channel.

attributes.name: format
attributes.description: The syntax the value is written in: `hex`, `rgb` or `hsl`.

attributes.name: no-format
attributes.description: Whether the reader may change the format from the panel.

attributes.name: placeholder
attributes.description: What the field says before a color is in it.

attributes.name: swatches
attributes.description: Colors offered under the picker, as a comma-separated list.

attributes.name: trigger-label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the control that opens the panel.

attributes.name: open
attributes.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

attributes.name: default-open
attributes.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

attributes.name: default-value
attributes.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

attributes.name: value
attributes.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

attributes.name: hint
attributes.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

attributes.name: feedback
attributes.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

attributes.name: required
attributes.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

attributes.name: disabled
attributes.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

attributes.description:

attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and

declarations.summary: A color, typed in any syntax or picked from a panel.

declarations.name: toRgb

type.text: { blue: number; green: number; red: number }

declarations.description: HSB to bytes, which is the road every written syntax goes down.

declarations.name: splitColors
declarations.description:
Splits a comma-separated list of colors, ignoring the commas inside them.

A plain `split(',')` is what this was, and it cannot hold the legacy syntaxes:
`#ef4444, rgb(249 115 22), rgba(34,197,94,.5)` came apart into six fragments,
four of them not colors, and the row quietly rendered three swatches instead
of four. The modern space-separated forms survived it, which is what made the
list look like it worked.

Depth rather than a regular expression, because the thing that matters is
whether a comma is inside a function call and that is exactly what a counter
answers. No color syntax nests, so a single counter is enough.

declarations.name: parseColor
declarations.description:
Any of the syntaxes to the working model, or `null` where it is not a color.

Named colors are not here. Resolving `rebeccapurple` means either shipping
the table of a hundred and forty or asking the browser, and the browser is not
present on the server: a field that accepted a name client-side and rejected
it during a server render would be worse than one that never took it.

declarations.name: formatColor
declarations.description:
The working model back out, in the syntax asked for.

The alpha is written only where the component carries one. A consumer who did
not ask for transparency should not have to strip `ff` off every hex or read
past a fourth argument they never wanted.

declarations.name: toCss
declarations.description: The color as CSS, for the swatches and the tracks. Always with its alpha.

**The picker itself, with no field around it.** Color Input is this element in
a panel behind a text field, the same way Date Input is `helix-date-picker` in a
panel: a form wants a field, and a settings pane or a toolbar wants the picker
sitting flat on the page with nothing to open. Neither should be the other one
with parts hidden.

**The square is two real range inputs.** Saturation and brightness are each an
`<input type="range">`, laid over the square and made invisible, and the
handle is drawn from their values. The pointer gets the square; the keyboard
gets the arrow keys, Home, End and the page keys; a screen reader gets two
sliders that announce a name and a number. All of it is the platform's, and
nothing here implements a key handler. There is no `role="application"`, which
is the usual way this control is built and amounts to asking a screen reader
to stop helping.

**The working model is HSB, and the value is derived from it.** The reverse
loses colors: black is `brightness: 0`, whose hue and saturation are both
undefined, so a reader who drags to the bottom of the square and back would
get gray where they had red. Holding the model means a color survives a trip
through one that has no hue. A value arriving from outside is read into the
model once, which is the only moment the conversion runs in that direction.

**Every syntax is read; the one `format` names is written.** `#f00`,
`#ff0000`, `rgb(255 0 0)`, `rgba(255,0,0,.5)` and `hsl(0 100% 50%)` are all
colors. Named colors are the exception, and deliberately: resolving
`rebeccapurple` means shipping a table of a hundred and forty or asking the
browser, and there is no browser during a server render.
declarations.name: HelixBaseColorPicker

members.name: invalid
members.description:
Whether the current selection fails validation.

A flag rather than a message, which is the split Date Picker already drew and
these two now follow. A flat picker has no room of its own for a sentence:
the field that wraps one owns the label, the hint and the feedback, and a
second message inside the panel would be the same error said twice. What is
left for the picker is the one thing the field cannot draw from outside, the
mark on the answer itself.

members.name: alpha
members.description:
Whether the color carries an alpha channel.

Off by default, because it widens every value written, and a consumer who
did not ask for transparency should not have to strip a byte off each one.

members.name: format
members.description:
The syntax the value is written in: `hex`, `rgb` or `hsl`.

Only what is written. Everything is read whatever this says, so a picker on
`hex` still takes an `rgb()` handed to it and stores the hex for it.

members.name: noValue
members.description:
Whether to leave the value out, for a picker whose value is stated elsewhere.

The row reads the color as text and lets it be typed or pasted, which is
what makes this element complete standing on a page: a square and two ramps
can build a color and cannot state one, and a reader who has a hex already
should not have to find it by dragging.

Color Input sets this, because its field is that input. Two editable fields
for one value is the outcome worth avoiding: two places to type, and no
answer to which one is authoritative or which has the caret. The other way
round was considered, Color Input dropping its own field and letting this be
the only one, and it is worse for a form: the value cannot be read or pasted
without opening a panel.

members.name: noFormat
members.description: Whether the reader may change the format.

members.name: noEyedropper
members.description: Whether the eyedropper is offered where the browser has one.

members.name: swatches
members.description: Colors offered under the picker, as a comma-separated list.

members.name: moved
members.description:
The color the reader has moved to, or nothing while they have moved none.

Held rather than re-read, which is the whole point: see the class
description. Cleared whenever a value arrives from anywhere else, so the
next reading comes from that value instead.

members.name: sampling
members.description:
Whether this browser can sample a color off the screen.

Settled after the first render rather than at construction, because there is
no `window` on the server, and a button that ships in the markup and does
nothing in Firefox is worse than one that is never offered.

members.name: owned
members.description:
Whether the value on this element was produced here.

The one bit that keeps the model from being overwritten by the value it just
produced. Without it, dragging to the bottom of the square writes black,
which reads back as hue 0 and saturation 0, and the next drag starts gray.

members.name: color
members.description: Where the picker stands: what was moved, or what the value says, or the start.

members.name: tools
members.description:
Whether the tools row holds anything at all.

The group is withheld rather than rendered empty, because it is an element
with a role and a name: an empty group labelled "Color tools" announces
nothing, and the footer cannot tell it is empty either, so the row kept its
padding with nothing in it.

members.name: presets
members.description: The presets, as written, with anything that is not a color dropped.

members.name: settled
members.description:
The last value that was a color.

Half-typed input reaches the row on every keystroke and most of it is not a
color, so the square is given the last thing that was one. Typing `#00ff00`
a character at a time goes `#`, `#0`, `#00`, `#00f`, `#00ff`, `#00ff0`,
`#00ff00`: two of those are colors and the ones between are not, so without
this the square walks red, blue, red, green. Color Input keeps the same
guard for its own field, each local to the input it protects.

members.name: handleValueInput
members.description: Takes what was typed, and lets the square follow only a whole color.

members.name: move
members.description: Moves part of the model and announces the value that follows from it.

members.name: copier
members.description:
Copying the value, which is the one thing here worth taking away.

A reader who has just built a color wants it in a stylesheet, and the
alternative is selecting text out of a field that may not be on screen. The
chip is the obvious target: it is the color, at the size of a control, and
it had no job at all before this.

The controller rather than the four lines it replaces, because a copy button
is coming and the two share everything that is easy to get wrong: the write,
the confirmation, the timer that ends it, the event, and a failure that is
correctly silent.

members.name: handleSwatch
members.description: Takes a preset, in this picker's syntax rather than as the preset spelled it.

members.name: handleFormat
members.description: Walks the format on, and rewrites the value in it.

members.name: handleEyeDropper
members.description:
Samples a color from anywhere on the screen.

`helix-sample-start` and `helix-sample-end` bracket it, because whatever is
holding this picker may need to get out of the way: `EyeDropper` takes the
pointer over, and a floating panel left up during it is one the reader
cannot dismiss and may well be trying to sample from underneath. This
element cannot know it is in a panel, so it says what it is doing and lets
whatever does know decide.

members.name: handleGridPointer
members.description:
Dragging in the square.

The two ranges are the state, so this reads a point and writes to them
rather than keeping a position of its own. Pointer capture, so a drag that
leaves the square keeps going: leaving and coming back is how a reader
reaches a corner, and without it the handle stops wherever the pointer left.

members.name: focus
members.description: Puts the keyboard on the square, which is the control a reader wants.

members.name: renderChannel
members.description: One of the ramps under the square.

members.name: renderTools
members.description:
The eyedropper and the swatch tools, which are a group of buttons, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

A method rather than a fragment inline, so a tier above can render its own,
wrap this one, pass it a property the base does not know about, or leave it
out, without reimplementing the whole template to do any of them. The
public tag rather than the base one: a consumer on the styled tier gets the
styled element, and one on the headless tier brings their own under that
name.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.description:
Whether the current selection fails validation.

A flag rather than a message, which is the split Date Picker already drew and
these two now follow. A flat picker has no room of its own for a sentence:
the field that wraps one owns the label, the hint and the feedback, and a
second message inside the panel would be the same error said twice. What is
left for the picker is the one thing the field cannot draw from outside, the
mark on the answer itself.

attributes.name: alpha
attributes.description:
Whether the color carries an alpha channel.

Off by default, because it widens every value written, and a consumer who
did not ask for transparency should not have to strip a byte off each one.

attributes.name: format
attributes.description:
The syntax the value is written in: `hex`, `rgb` or `hsl`.

Only what is written. Everything is read whatever this says, so a picker on
`hex` still takes an `rgb()` handed to it and stores the hex for it.

attributes.name: no-value
attributes.description:
Whether to leave the value out, for a picker whose value is stated elsewhere.

The row reads the color as text and lets it be typed or pasted, which is
what makes this element complete standing on a page: a square and two ramps
can build a color and cannot state one, and a reader who has a hex already
should not have to find it by dragging.

Color Input sets this, because its field is that input. Two editable fields
for one value is the outcome worth avoiding: two places to type, and no
answer to which one is authoritative or which has the caret. The other way
round was considered, Color Input dropping its own field and letting this be
the only one, and it is worse for a form: the value cannot be read or pasted
without opening a panel.

attributes.name: no-format
attributes.description: Whether the reader may change the format.

attributes.name: default-value
attributes.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

attributes.name: value
attributes.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects

attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and

declarations.summary: Picks a color, from a square and two ramps.

declarations.description:
**The list is `helix-listbox`, and the filtering is its own.** It already
owns narrowing, the empty state, the highlight, `aria-activedescendant` and
scrolling an option into view, and every one of those is a decision with a
long note attached. Rewriting them here would be a second copy to keep in
step; what is left for this element is the field, the panel and the traffic
between them.

**The text and the value are two things.** What a reader types is a filter,
not an answer: it narrows the list and is thrown away. The value is whichever
option they then choose, and the field is rewritten to that option's words
once they have. A combobox that treated the typing as the value would submit
"jav" to a form, which is the mistake a plain input makes and the reason this
component exists.

That is also why the field is emptied of its filter on close rather than left
holding it: a control reopened still narrowed by the last visit's search is a
control whose second use starts from the first one's leftovers. Select
records the same, having been fixed for it.

**Focus stays in the field, which is the whole of what a combobox is.** The
arrows move the list without leaving the text, which is why the listbox has a
public `navigate`: the moving, the wrapping, the skipping of disabled options
and the seeding from the current value all stay in the one place that already
does them.

`role="combobox"` on the input rather than on a wrapper, because the thing
the pattern describes is the text field, and `aria-controls` can name the
listbox because both are in this shadow root. The active option cannot be
named that way, being the consumer's light DOM, so it is linked by element
reference for the reason Listbox records at length.
declarations.name: HelixBaseCombobox

members.name: placeholder
members.description: Text shown while nothing has been chosen.

members.name: multiple
members.description:
Whether more than one option can be chosen.

The list already does the work: `value` comes apart on commas, a press
toggles rather than replaces, and the arrows move without choosing. What
this adds is the tags, and keeping the panel open between picks.

A comma is therefore not available inside an option's value, which is the
listbox's contract and not this element's to change.

members.name: creatable
members.description:
Whether the reader may answer with something the list does not hold.

The row appears while what is typed matches no option's words exactly, so
it is offered next to near misses too: a reader typing "Ruby on Rails" with
"Ruby" in the list wants the one they are typing, not the one they are
halfway through.

members.name: suggest
members.description:
Whether the field finishes the word as it is typed.

`suggest` rather than `autocomplete`, which is a real HTML attribute this
element already sets on the input it renders, and two things of one name
meaning different things on the same control is a question a consumer
should not have to ask.

members.name: createLabel
members.description: What the create row says, before the words it would add.

members.name: removeLabel
members.description: What a tag's remove control is called, since the mark has no name.

members.name: maxTags
members.description:
How many tags to draw before the rest become a count. `multiple` only.

`0` is all of them, and is the default: a cap that guesses is worse than no
cap, because the number that fits depends on the width of the field and the
length of what is in it, neither of which this element knows. What a cap is
genuinely for is a field in a row or a table cell, where a set of twelve
choices would push everything below it down a line at a time.

The remainder is counted rather than hidden. `+3` is a fact a reader can act
on, where a row that silently stops is a field that appears to have lost
what was put in it. Date Input and Time Input carry the same property and
the same reasoning.

members.name: listLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the list, which has no visible one of its own.

members.name: loading
members.description:
Whether the options are still on their way.

Passed straight to the list, which is where the rows are and so where the
message belongs.

members.name: loadingText
members.description: What the list says while they are on their way.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: Words shown where the filter has hidden everything.

members.name: typed
members.description:
What the reader has typed, which narrows the list and is not the value.

State rather than a property, because it is a keystroke rather than API: a
consumer sets `value` to say what is chosen, and nothing outside needs to
say what is half-typed.

members.name: suggestion
members.description:
The completed words, where the field is finishing one, and empty otherwise.

Held apart from `typed` rather than replacing it, because they are needed
for different things at the same moment: this one is what the input shows,
`typed` is what the list is filtered by, and the selection between them is
what the reader is offered.

members.name: panel
members.default: new PopoverController(this, { anchor: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="field"]'), /* The surface *and* the field, for the reason four components here were fixed for: scoped to the surface alone, a press on the field counts as outside, so `pointerdown` closes the panel and the field's own handler reopens it on the `click` that follows. */ boundary: (): readonly (Element | null | undefined)[] => [ this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="surface"]'), this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="field"]'), ], offset: () => 4, onDismiss: () => this.close(), placement: 'bottom-start', surface: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="surface"]'), })

members.name: values
members.description: The values chosen, in the order they were chosen.

members.name: chosen
members.description:
The chosen options themselves, for their words.

Read off the options rather than stored, because the words are the
consumer's content and a copy of them goes stale the moment they change it.
Select records the same.

In the value's own order, which is the order they were chosen. It has to
be: a created answer is not in the list at all, so there is no position in
the list to give it. Neither order ever reshuffles what is already there,
so a tag does not move out from under the pointer about to remove it.

members.name: showing
members.description:
Whether the filter has left anything to choose.

Read off the options rather than asked of the listbox, which keeps its own
answer to this private. Both come from the same place: `hidden` is what the
filter writes onto an option, and it is public because hiding one by hand
is a thing a consumer may do.

members.name: creation
members.description:
What the create row would add, or nothing where there is nothing to add.

Empty where the words already name an option exactly, case aside: offering
to add "Rust" under a list showing "Rust" is offering the reader a second
copy of what they are looking at.

members.name: create
members.description:
Takes what the reader typed as an answer, once anyone listening allows it.

Added to the set with `multiple` and replacing it without, which is the
same rule choosing an option follows: what differs about a created answer
is where it came from, not how many the field holds.

members.name: shown
members.description: The choices that get a tag, which is all of them until `maxTags` says not.

members.name: restCount
members.description: How many are held beyond the ones shown.

members.name: word
members.description: What a single-choice field shows at rest, which the tags replace.

members.name: drop
members.description:
Takes one value out of the set, which is what a tag's remove control does.

`drop` rather than `remove`, which every element already has: `Element`
defines `remove()` and a method of that name here would be overriding it,
so `combobox.remove()` would stop taking the combobox out of the document.

members.name: completionFor
members.description:
The words of the first option the typing begins, or nothing.

Case-insensitively matched and returned in the option's own case, so a
reader typing "ru" is offered "Rust" rather than "rust": the completion is
a name from the list, and correcting the reader's capitals to match it is
the whole point of showing it.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
The keys the field answers, and the ones it hands on.

Everything that moves within the list goes to the list, which is what
`navigate` is for. Escape and Tab are the field's, because they are about
the panel rather than about the options in it.

members.name: handleChange
members.description:
Takes what the list announced and stops it there.

The listbox says `helix-change` under its own name, and a consumer
listening on this element would otherwise hear two changes for one choice,
one of them naming a control they did not put on the page.

members.name: handleFieldClick
members.description:
Anywhere in the field opens the list, and puts the caret where typing goes.

On the field rather than on the `<input>`, which is where it was. The caret
is a sibling of the input and so is the tag strip, so pressing the one part
of the control that visibly says "this opens" did nothing at all, and a
reader who wanted the list had to find the text box. Anything drawn inside
the field is the field.

A tag is the exception, because a tag is its own control: its dismiss
removes a choice, and opening the list on the way past would leave the
reader looking at a panel they did not ask for. Read from the composed
path, since the press lands on a button inside the tag's shadow root and
the event has retargeted by the time it arrives here.

It only ever opens. Closing is Escape, a choice, or leaving, which is what
the input already did and what a text field wants: a control that closed
when you clicked into the middle of your own typing would be unusable.

members.name: handleDismiss
members.description: One tag asking to be taken out of the set.

members.name: sync
members.description:
Reports the answer and the verdict on it.

The value rather than the typed text, which is the whole point of the
component: a form that received "jav" got the filter, not an option.

members.name: renderListbox
members.description:
The list the field filters, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

A method rather than a fragment inline, so a tier above can render its own,
wrap this one, pass it a property the base does not know about, or leave it
out, without reimplementing the whole template to do any of them. The
public tag rather than the base one: a consumer on the styled tier gets the
styled element, and one on the headless tier brings their own under that
name.

members.name: renderTag
members.description:
One chosen option, as a tag, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

A method rather than a fragment inline, so a tier above can render its own,
wrap this one, pass it a property the base does not know about, or leave it
out, without reimplementing the whole template to do any of them. The
public tag rather than the base one: a consumer on the styled tier gets the
styled element, and one on the headless tier brings their own under that
name.

members.name: renderIndicator
members.description:
The caret saying the field opens, behind a seam.

Slot fallback, so a consumer replaces it by slotting; and a method, so the
tier above replaces it by overriding. Those answer different people: the
slot is for the page and the method is for whoever is building the styled
layer, and a fallback with only the first is one a tier can restyle and
cannot change.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.
