attributes.name: open
attributes.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

declarations.description:
Determinate by default, and `indeterminate` for a task whose total is not
known yet. `Loader` is still the right answer where the wait is short or has
no place of its own on the page; a bar earns its width where the work is the
subject of the region it sits in.

A bar that fills at a made-up rate would be a bar that lies, so the
indeterminate one does not fill: it runs a segment across the track, which
says work is happening and claims no proportion at all. `aria-valuenow` is
omitted with it, which is the platform's own signal for the same thing.

**The fill is a percentage of the track, written as a custom property.** It
is derived from `value` and `max` rather than measured, so it renders on a
server with no layout and needs nothing after upgrade. That is what keeps it
out of the class of geometry this library writes only on the client.

**`value` is clamped, and out-of-range input is not an error.** A count that
runs past its own total is ordinary in real applications, and a bar that
overflows its track or reports `aria-valuenow` above `aria-valuemax` is worse
than one that reads as finished.

Semantics are on the host through `ElementInternals`, the same as everywhere
else: a `role` in the shadow root announces correctly and leaves the host
anonymous to anything walking the light DOM, and a `role` written onto the
host as an attribute is one a server's markup never had.

declarations.description:
**The picture is one `<path>`, not a grid of squares.** A code of any useful
length is a thousand modules, and drawing each as its own rect is a thousand
nodes for one image. Runs of adjacent dark modules are joined, so a row of
eight is one horizontal move rather than eight squares.

**It is an image and says so.** `role="img"` with a name, because what a
reader with a screen reader needs is what the code is *for*, and no amount of
describing the pattern gives them that. Where nothing is passed the value
itself is the name, which is right far more often than it looks: most codes
hold a URL, and a URL read aloud is the destination.

**The quiet zone is part of the code.** Four modules of margin are required
by the specification, not a design choice, and a scanner will refuse a code
that is cropped to its edge. It is drawn inside the `viewBox` so it survives
any size the component is given, including one set in CSS.

`correction` is what buys the middle slot. A code at `H` can lose thirty
percent of itself and still read, which is what makes covering the centre
with a mark safe; at `L` the same mark makes the code unscannable. That is
why the slot exists on the same element as the property, and why the default
moves when the slot is filled.

members.name: value
members.description: What the code encodes, which is usually a URL.

members.name: label
members.description:
What the image is called.

Falling back to the value is deliberate: a code almost always holds a URL,
and a URL is a better name than "QR code" for a reader who cannot see it.

members.name: shape
members.description:
How the modules are drawn.

`square` is the default and the only one that joins runs of adjacent
modules into a single subpath, which is what keeps a thousand modules to a
handful of nodes. `rounded` and `dots` draw each module on its own, because
the corners are the thing being drawn and a joined run has none in the
middle. That cost is paid only by a code that asks for them.

A scanner reads contrast between cells, not their shape, so all three
scan. `dots` sits a little under half a module so neighbours do not touch,
which is what makes it read as dots rather than as a softened square code.

members.name: correction
members.description:
How much of the code can be lost and still read.

`M` by default, which is the level almost every code in the world uses and
costs about fifteen percent redundancy. `H` where a mark covers the centre,
chosen automatically when the slot is filled: it is the level that makes
covering safe, and a consumer who fills the slot has said what they want
without having to know that.

declarations.description:
**The group is the control, and the radios are its options.** This is the
asymmetry with checkboxes and it comes from what a form submits: a set of
checkboxes is several answers and each box submits its own, while a set of
radios is one answer, so the group owns the `name`, the `value` and the
validity, and a lone radio outside a group is not a control at all.

Which is also why `MixinField` lands here and not on `Radio`: the label, the
hint and the message are about the question, and the question is the set.

Selection travels up and state travels down. An item announces that it was
chosen, the group decides whether that stands, and the group writes
`selected` onto every item. Nothing sets itself, so there is one answer to
"which one is on" rather than one per item.

`value` and `defaultValue` are separate for the reason `checked` and
`defaultChecked` are: `value` is the answer now, `defaultValue` is what the
markup asked for, which is where a reset returns and is gone the moment
anything is chosen.

members.name: handleSelection
members.description:
Announces before it applies, so a listener can refuse the change.

The item has not moved by the time this runs, unlike a native input, so
refusing is simply not writing the value: there is nothing to put back.

members.name: place
members.description: Writes the answer onto the items, and nothing onto the host.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the answer and the verdict on it.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.description:
Renders a `<button role="radio">`, not an `<input type="radio">`, and the
reason is the shadow boundary rather than preference: native radios group by
sharing a `name` within a form, and a radio inside a shadow root cannot join
a group on the other side of it. The group is the form control here, so the
option only has to say what it is and announce when it is chosen.

**It carries no label of its own.** A radio is named by the words beside it,
which is its own content, and the label, hint and message of the *set* belong
to the group. This is the one control in the family that takes nothing from
`MixinField`, because a lone radio is not a control: it is an answer to one.

Selection is announced rather than applied. The item dispatches, the group
decides, and the group writes `selected` back. An item that set itself would
be a second source of truth for which one is on.

declarations.summary: One choice in a radio group.

declarations.description:
**Half marks decide the shape, so they are decided first.** Supporting them
means the value is not an integer and the targets are not the marks: five
stars at a half step is ten places to press, and a mark that is filled to the
middle. Everything else follows from that, which is why `step` is here rather
than added later, when the pointer handling would have to be rewritten around
it.

**A partial mark is the whole mark, clipped.** Not a second glyph filled to
the middle: that needs a matching pair drawn for every mark anybody uses, and
the moment a consumer wants a heart or a circle they need to draw one too. The
fill is the same marks over the same marks, cut off partway, so any mark works
and any fraction does.

**Read-only is not this control greyed out, it is a different thing.** The
commoner use is showing a score nobody is being asked for, a product's
average, and that is not a control at all: it takes no focus, answers no keys,
has no options to choose between, and reads as one thing rather than as five.
So `readonly` is `role="img"` with the score in its name, where the control is
a radio group. A disabled control is still a control and still says so; this
is not one.

**Moving is choosing here**, which is the radio group's reading and the
opposite of `Menu`'s: arriving at four stars *is* rating it four, because
nothing else follows and there is nothing to confirm. That is what
`KeyboardNavigationController` takes `selects` for, and why this can use it
where a menu cannot.

members.name: step
members.description:
The smallest part of a mark that can be chosen.

`0.5` is the half star, and it is the reason the value is a number rather
than an index: with halves, five marks are ten answers.

members.name: readOnly
members.description:
Whether this shows a score rather than asks for one.

A readout is not a control that has been switched off. It takes no focus,
answers no keys, and reads as one thing: see the note on the class.

members.name: valueText
members.description:
How the score is read out, where "3.5 out of 5" is not what it should say.

A rating out of five is one of the few places a screen reader gets a worse
answer from the value than from a sentence: "3.5" alone is a number without
a subject. This names the readout, where a control is named by its `label`
and each of its options by the score that option is.

members.name: showValue
members.description:
Whether the score is written out beside the marks.

Marks say roughly, and a number says exactly. Four and a bit stars is not a
reading anyone can repeat, which is why a product's average is nearly always
printed next to them. `Meter` spells its reading the same way and under the
same attribute.

It follows the pointer, because it labels what the marks are showing rather
than what the form holds: a label that disagreed with the marks under the
reader's own cursor would be worse than no label.

members.name: markSource
members.description:
The shape a consumer slotted, if they slotted one.

Read rather than projected. A `<slot>` shows its content once and a rating
needs the shape as many times as there are marks, twice over because there
are two layers, so the slot here is a way of being handed the shape rather
than a place the shape is drawn. What is handed over gets cloned into every
position.

**One shape, not one per position.** A rating is a quantity of identical
marks and the fill is a clip across all of them, so a row whose third mark
is a different drawing from its first is not a rating: it is a set of
choices, which is `Radio.Group` and already carries a value and a name on
each of its own options. Anything past the first slotted element is
ignored.

members.name: previewing
members.description: What the pointer is over, which is shown instead of the score while it is.

members.name: keys
members.default: new KeyboardNavigationController(this, { items: () => this.options, selects: () => true, wrap: false, })

members.name: score
members.description: The score, as a number, clamped to what the marks can show.

members.name: steps
members.description: Every score a reader can choose, which is `max / step` of them.

members.name: options
members.description:
The options, as the shared controller wants them.

Adapters rather than elements, because these are buttons this element drew
rather than a consumer's custom elements: the interface asks for five
things and a `<button>` in a shadow root can answer all five without being
dressed up as a component to do it.

members.name: dragging
members.description: The pointer drawing a score, while one is.

members.name: clones
members.description:
One clone per place a mark goes, kept so a render does not remake them.

A drag renders on every pointer move, and handing Lit a fresh node each
time would swap every mark in the row on every frame of a gesture whose
whole point is that only the fill moves.

members.name: markFor
members.description: The shape for one place, or nothing when the stylesheet is drawing it.

members.name: scoreAt
members.description:
The step under a point on the row, or the nearest one to it.

Asked of the boxes rather than worked out from `max` and `step`, because
where a step sits is the stylesheet's arithmetic and this would be a second
copy of it that could disagree. The browser has already laid the targets
out; this reads them back.

Nearest rather than only a hit, so a drag that runs off the end of the row
pins to the last mark instead of stopping at whatever it last touched, and
a pointer in the half-gap outside the first mark still answers.

members.name: handleDragStart
members.description:
Dragging across the marks draws a score, and letting go chooses it.

One press and a slide is how a rating is given on a phone, and on a desktop
it is how somebody who overshoots corrects without lifting. Pointer capture
is what makes it one gesture: without it the events go to whichever target
the pointer crossed into, and a drag that leaves the row stops reporting.

Nothing is chosen until release, so a drag that ends back where it started,
or off the element entirely, has asked for nothing.

members.description:

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is

decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: feedback

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:

browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

getting to the one that matters.

until yesterday.

arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.summary: A score out of a few marks, given or shown.

declarations.name: EDGES
declarations.description: Which edges have something past them, as a set of tokens.

**The whole component is one fact a stylesheet cannot work out for itself:
which edges have content past them.** A fade at the bottom of a list is easy
to draw and impossible to decide, because CSS has no reading of scroll
position. So this measures and says, in `data-more`, and the styled tier
draws whatever it likes on the edges named.

**Tokens rather than four attributes**, so a stylesheet asks
`[data-more~="block-end"]` the way it would ask about a class. Four booleans
say the same thing in four selectors and read worse at every use.

**A scrolling region takes the keyboard when it scrolls, and not before.**
A box a reader can only reach with a pointer is a box some readers cannot
read at all, which is what `tabindex` answers here. Only while it overflows:
a tab stop on a box with nothing to scroll is a stop that does nothing, and a
form full of them is worse than the problem.

`role="region"` only with a `label`, because an unnamed region is an
announcement with no content: a screen reader says "region" and the reader
has learned nothing they did not already know.

members.name: scroller
members.description:
The box that actually scrolls, for anything that needs to move it.

**Public because the alternative is silence.** Bringing a row into view
means telling a scroll utility which box to scroll, and the scrolling box
here is inside a shadow root: a consumer holding a reference to this
element holds the host, which does not scroll, and `scrollBy` on it is a
no-op that reports nothing. That is exactly how `scrollItemIntoView`'s
`offsetParent` default fails, and the sandbox sidebar spent an afternoon
scrolled to zero because of it.

The element rather than a method of our own, because the utilities that
want it already take one, and `Tree`, `Combobox` and anything windowing a
long list all want the same thing from it.

members.name: measure
members.description:
Reads the four edges off the box.

A pixel of slack on each, because a scroller at its end is routinely a
fraction short of it: browsers round scroll positions differently under
zoom and on a display that is not at one to one, and a fade that never
quite goes out at the bottom of a fully scrolled list is the bug that
costs.

declarations.summary: A scrolling box that says there is more.

declarations.description:
**A trigger and a `Listbox`, not a listbox reimplemented behind a button.**
The list this opens is the same element a consumer can use on its own, with
the same keyboard, the same filtering and the same multi-select rules. What
Select adds is the closing: a trigger that says what is chosen, a surface
that floats, and somewhere for focus to go back to.

The options are the consumer's, in the consumer's light DOM, slotted through
into the listbox. That is why the listbox walks through slots to find them:
from its point of view the options belong to something else.

**What it does not do is duplicate the value.** `Select` owns it, hands it
down, and takes changes back; the listbox is the thing being operated and not
a second place the answer lives.

was never read: it reflected, it type-checked, and nothing anywhere

members.description:
Whether the options are still on their way.

Passed straight to the list, which is where the rows are and so where the
message belongs. Two components saying "Loading" about one request is a
consumer wiring the same flag twice.

members.description: Shown on the trigger while nothing is chosen.

members.name: listbox
members.description:
The list inside the surface, or nothing where there is no DOM to hold one.

The optional chain is the server. `renderRoot` is a property Lit's element
shim does not carry, and this getter is reached from `display`, which is
read during `render`: without it the select threw on every server render
and could not be served at all. Found by writing its SSR spec, which is
the only thing that would have found it, because the client is where every
other path runs and the client always has a root.

The other reads of `renderRoot` here are inside callbacks the controllers
invoke, and a controller only runs on a connected element, so they cannot
be reached from the server and are left plain.

members.name: panel
members.default: new PopoverController(this, { anchor: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="trigger"]'), /* The surface *and* the trigger. * * A control is not always one element: the button that opens this panel is * part of it, and a press on it is not a press outside. Scoped to the * surface alone, `pointerdown` on the trigger closed the panel and the * trigger's own `toggleOpen` reopened it on the `click` that followed, so * the panel could never be closed by the button that opened it. Measured * across all five popover-bearing components: Menu, Popover and Tooltip * already named their invoker; this one and its three siblings did not, and * all four stayed open on a second press where Menu closed. * * `DismissController` documents this exact failure and takes a list for it. * The list was the fix; using it was the part that did not happen here. */ boundary: (): readonly (Element | null | undefined)[] => [ this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="surface"]'), this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="trigger"]'), ], offset: () => 4, onDismiss: () => this.close(), placement: 'bottom-start', surface: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="surface"]'), })

What the trigger says: the chosen options' words, or the placeholder.

Read off the options rather than stored, because the words are the

members.description: Closes the list and puts focus back where it came from.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the answer and the verdict on it.

members.name: renderListbox
members.description:
The list the trigger opens, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

A method rather than a fragment inline, so a tier above can render its own
list, wrap this one, or pass it a property the base does not know about,
without reimplementing the whole template. The public tag rather than the
base one: a consumer on the styled tier gets the styled listbox, and one on
the headless tier brings a listbox of their own under that name.

members.name: renderIndicator
members.description:
The caret saying the control opens, behind a seam.

Slot fallback, so a consumer replaces it by slotting; and a method, so the
tier above replaces it by overriding. Those answer different people: the
slot is for the page and the method is for whoever is building the styled
layer, and a fallback with only the first is one a tier can restyle and
cannot change.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the

members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

attributes.name: open
attributes.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it

attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element

property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all

writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute

opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing

means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

declarations.summary: Stands in for content that has not arrived.

declarations.description:
A real `<input type="range">`, so the drag, the arrow keys, Home and End, the
page keys and the touch target are all the platform's. Every one of those is
a thing a hand-built slider gets wrong, and the last is the one nobody
notices: a native range has a hit area larger than its thumb, sized by the
platform for a finger.

**The value is a string, like every other form control's.** A range submits
text and `MixinControllerValue` holds text, so the number is a reading of the
value rather than the value itself. `valueAsNumber` is there for anything
doing arithmetic on it.

**Marks are drawn rather than left to `<datalist>`**, which was the first
answer and is the wrong one. A datalist's ticks cannot be styled at all, and
Firefox does not render them for a range at all, so the platform's version is
a mark that looks like someone else's design where it appears and no mark
where it does not. Drawing them costs the semantics nothing, because a mark
is decoration: what a reader can actually land on is `step`, which the input
enforces whether or not anything is drawn.

`markers` is a count rather than a flag tied to `step`. A flag reads well
until a slider from zero to a hundred stepping by one asks for a hundred and
one ticks, and then it is either noise or a silent refusal to draw. A number
is what the reader sees, so it cannot surprise anyone.

**A range is two of them, not a hand-built one.** There is no native
two-thumb range, and the answer is not to stop using the platform's: it is to
stack two of them on one track, so each thumb keeps its own drag, its own
arrow keys, its own Home and End and its own finger-sized hit area. Rebuilding
would throw away every argument this component is made of, to gain a second
handle.

Crossing is stopped in the handler rather than by the bounds, and that is not
the obvious way round. Giving the lower input `max` of the upper reads well
and breaks the drawing: an input's thumb sits at a fraction of *its own*
range, so a lower thumb bounded at the upper one paints against a shorter
track and the two stop lining up. Both inputs span the whole range and the
values are clamped against each other on the way in.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Typed or dragged, so every edit is announced. See `announcesInput`.

members.name: range
members.description:
Whether there are two thumbs and the value is a pair.

The pair is one string, `"10,50"`, which is what a form submits and what
`MixinControllerValue` already holds. `valueAsNumber` reads the lower of
the two, since a range has no single number.

members.name: max
members.description: The largest value the reader can choose.

members.name: min
members.description: The smallest value the reader can choose.

members.name: showValue
members.description: Whether the chosen value is shown beside the track.

members.name: markers
members.description:
How many marks to draw along the track, evenly spaced, ends included.

`0` or `1` draws none: one mark on a track says nothing about a range.
They are decoration, so they are `aria-hidden`; what a reader can land on
is `step`, which the input enforces regardless.

**Each one is snapped to a step before it is placed.** Evenly spaced and
on a step are two different things, and asking for four marks across a
hundred in twenty-fives wants them at 0, 33.3, 66.7 and 100: two of those
are places the thumb cannot go. A mark the thumb can never sit on is the
one thing a mark must not be, so the spacing gives way rather than the
step, and marks may come out unevenly spaced when the two disagree. That
is the honest picture of the range being offered.

members.name: markerLabels
members.description:
Mirrors "there are marks" for the stylesheet.

The whole marker layout hung off `:host([markers])` and `markers` does not
reflect, so `slider.markers = 5` drew nothing at all: only the attribute
written in the markup ever worked, and the property that is the documented
API silently did not.

Reflecting the count instead would put `markers="0"` on every slider, an
attribute the server's markup does not have and one that selector would
match, drawing the layout for no marks. So the boolean fact is mirrored to
a `data-` name, which is the rule this library already follows for state:
the stylesheet wants to know whether there are marks, not how many. How
many is what `markerValues` answers, and `< 2` is where it already draws
the line.

/** Whether each mark says which value it stands at.

members.name: step
members.description: How far one press of an arrow key moves it.

members.name: precision
members.description:
How many decimals the step is written to, so a label is not float noise.

`min + index * step` on a fractional step prints `0.30000000000000004`,
which is arithmetic being honest and a label being wrong. Rounding back to
the step's own precision is what the reader asked for when they wrote it.

members.name: valueAsNumber
members.description: The chosen value as a number, for anything doing arithmetic on it.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Focus is delegated to the control, so the host is never the target.

members.name: bounds
members.description:
The pair, as numbers, in order.

Falls back to the whole range rather than to zero, so a range slider given
no value opens fully wide instead of pinned shut at its own minimum, which
is what a filter with nothing filtered out looks like.

members.name: along
members.description: Where one value sits along the track, as a fraction of it.

members.name: handleChange
members.description: Relayed, because `change` does not cross a shadow boundary on its own.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the value.

members.name: fraction
members.description:
How far along the track the thumb sits, as a fraction.

Arithmetic rather than a measurement, because the browser already knows
where it drew the handle and measuring it would be a guess at that.

**Sanitized here, not read back off the control.** This asked the input for
its value, on the reasoning that a range clamps and snaps whatever it is
given, so the control is the truth about where the thumb is. The reasoning
is right and the timing is not: `fraction` is evaluated inside `render()`,
and the `style` binding carrying it is committed *before* the `.value`
binding below it, so it read the value this very render was about to
replace. The fill was a render behind the thumb, and on the first pass it
read the seeded midpoint and stayed there.

Measured on a slider from 0 to 1: after dragging to either end, the host's
`value` was `1`, the control's was `1`, and `--_slider-fraction` was still
`0.5`. Off by half a track, and stable, which is what made it look like a
drawing bug rather than a timing one.

So the same two operations a range performs are done here: snap to the step
from `min`, then clamp to the bounds. Nothing is read from the tree, so
there is no order for this to be on the wrong side of.

members.name: snapped
members.description:
A value snapped to the step, counted from `min` the way a range counts it.

`min` rather than zero is the whole of it: a slider from `0.2` with a step
of `0.05` can land on `0.2`, `0.25` and so on, and snapping against zero
would offer `0.2` and `0.25` too but round the ones between to the wrong
side. `precision` is what keeps `0.30000000000000004` off the track, the
same guard the marker labels already use.

members.name: orientation
members.description:
Which way the track runs, `vertical` standing it on end.

For a level rather than a quantity: a fader, a channel, anything a reader
pictures as high and low rather than as less and more. Absent is
horizontal, which is what almost every slider in a form wants.

**A vertical track has no length of its own**, the way a horizontal one
takes the width of the row it is in. `--slider-length` is that number and
defaults to nine rem, so one dropped into a layout is a usable height
rather than a thumb sitting on nothing.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it

`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates

Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback

Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel

A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.
