members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: internals

The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

attributes.description:
Whether there are two thumbs and the value is a pair.

The pair is one string, `"10,50"`, which is what a form submits and what
`MixinControllerValue` already holds. `valueAsNumber` reads the lower of
the two, since a range has no single number.

attributes.name: min

attributes.description: Whether the chosen value is shown beside the track.

attributes.name: markers
attributes.description:
How many marks to draw along the track, evenly spaced, ends included.

`0` or `1` draws none: one mark on a track says nothing about a range.
They are decoration, so they are `aria-hidden`; what a reader can land on
is `step`, which the input enforces regardless.

**Each one is snapped to a step before it is placed.** Evenly spaced and
on a step are two different things, and asking for four marks across a
hundred in twenty-fives wants them at 0, 33.3, 66.7 and 100: two of those
are places the thumb cannot go. A mark the thumb can never sit on is the
one thing a mark must not be, so the spacing gives way rather than the
step, and marks may come out unevenly spaced when the two disagree. That
is the honest picture of the range being offered.

attributes.name: marker-labels
attributes.description:
Mirrors "there are marks" for the stylesheet.

The whole marker layout hung off `:host([markers])` and `markers` does not
reflect, so `slider.markers = 5` drew nothing at all: only the attribute
written in the markup ever worked, and the property that is the documented
API silently did not.

Reflecting the count instead would put `markers="0"` on every slider, an
attribute the server's markup does not have and one that selector would
match, drawing the layout for no marks. So the boolean fact is mirrored to
a `data-` name, which is the rule this library already follows for state:
the stylesheet wants to know whether there are marks, not how many. How
many is what `markerValues` answers, and `< 2` is where it already draws
the line.

/** Whether each mark says which value it stands at.

attributes.description: How far one press of an arrow key moves it.

attributes.name: orientation
attributes.description:
Which way the track runs, `vertical` standing it on end.

For a level rather than a quantity: a fader, a channel, anything a reader
pictures as high and low rather than as less and more. Absent is
horizontal, which is what almost every slider in a form wants.

**A vertical track has no length of its own**, the way a horizontal one
takes the width of the row it is in. `--slider-length` is that number and
defaults to nine rem, so one dropped into a layout is a usable height
rather than a thumb sitting on nothing.

attributes.name: value
attributes.description:

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what

means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

declarations.summary: A value chosen from a range by dragging.

declarations.description:
The one chart here that takes its numbers from an attribute, and the reversal
is deliberate. Every other chart reads a table because a reader might want to
interrogate it; nobody interrogates the squiggle next to a figure. A
fourteen-row table behind a bare trend line is fourteen dates read aloud in
place of the one sentence that carries the meaning, so `values` is the list
and `label` is the sentence.

That is the library's own rule rather than a second data channel: a content
property is its slot's fallback, which is why `Tooltip` takes `content` and
`Avatar` takes `name`. `for` stays for the sparkline that genuinely has a
table behind it, and it wins where both are given.

**No label means decorative, and that is a choice rather than an oversight.**
A sparkline beside a stat that already says "Sessions, 1,102" has nothing of
its own to announce, and an unnamed `role="img"` announces "graphic" and
stops. So an unlabelled sparkline is `aria-hidden`, and a labelled one is an
image named by its sentence.

It goes *beside* a `Stat` rather than inside one. The plan this was built
from called for a `trend` slot on `Stat`; the spec already on `Stat` says the
opposite, that a change beside a figure is a second fact, and the spec is
right. `Trend` composes the same way.

members.name: plot
members.description:
What the readings are drawn as.

Absent is a line, `area` is a line with the region beneath it washed, and
`bar` is a column per reading.

**A bar plot measures from zero and the other two measure from the data's
own range**, which is the one way the plots are not interchangeable. A line
says where the readings sit relative to each other, so a scale over their
extent uses the whole box and claims nothing about absolute size. A bar's
length *is* the value, so any baseline but zero makes the lengths
proportional to nothing.

**Which is a reason to prefer a line for readings in a narrow band far from
zero.** Seven values between 1,102 and 1,408 drawn as columns from zero are
seven columns of nearly the same height, and that is the true picture: they
*are* nearly the same. The same readings as a line fill the box and show
the movement, because a line is only ever claiming a shape.

**Absent is `area`**, which is the departure from the rule that a resting
arrangement is the plainest thing. At the size a sparkline is actually
drawn, a hairline in a wide box is mostly box: the wash under it is what
gives the shape a body and lets a reader see it at a glance rather than
hunting for it, which is the entire job. `line` is the bare stroke for
anywhere the fill would be noise, several of them in one box for instance.

This tier rather than the one above: a plot type is geometry and geometry
is markup, the same reason `curve` lives here.

members.name: curve
members.description:
How the line gets from one reading to the next.

Absent joins them and claims nothing in between, which is why it is the
default. `smooth` is easier to follow across a long series and invents the
values between the readings; it is monotone cubic, so what it invents never
leaves the band the data sets. `step` claims the opposite, that a reading
holds until the next. Bars ignore it, having no between to interpolate.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of a table to read instead, when there is one behind the line.

The first column of numbers is the series drawn. This wins over `values`,
because a table is the readable representation and a list of numbers in an
attribute is not.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: label
members.description:
What the line says, in a sentence.

"Sessions rose from 1,240 to 1,318 and fell to 1,102 over fourteen days" is
the accessible representation of a sparkline, and a list of the fourteen
numbers is not. Absent, the drawing is hidden from a screen reader rather
than announced without a name.

members.name: values
members.description:
The numbers, separated by whitespace or by commas.

Both separators, so `values="1240 1318"` and an array assigned to the
property both work: assigning `[1240, 1318]` stringifies to `1240,1318`,
and a string is what survives React's hydration where an array property
does not.

declarations.description:
**A command, which is why this is a `menuitem` and a megamenu's rows are not.**
The distinction is what the thing does, not what it looks like: a megamenu
holds destinations, so it is a disclosure of links, and this holds actions a
screen can take, which is exactly what `role="menu"` was written for. The
roles follow the contents.

**The name is text, not a title.** A dial's actions are icons, and an icon
with a `title` is an action whose name only exists for whoever hovers it long
enough. The label is rendered beside the mark and is the accessible name by
being there, so it is read, searched and translated like anything else.

declarations.description:
**A menu, and deliberately not a new one.** Its rows are commands, which is
what `role="menu"` and `menuitem` exist for, so this takes them and takes the
behaviour with them: the arrow keys are `KeyboardNavigationController`, the
panel is `PopoverController`, and open and closed is `MixinControllerOpen`.
`Menu` is built from the same pieces. What is not shared is what actually
differs: a dial has no submenus, no headers, no checkable rows and no long
list to type ahead through, and shipping it as an appearance of `Menu` would
have meant defining what a dial with a submenu in it does.

**The trigger is a control the consumer slots**, and the floating action
button is the usual one: `helix-icon-button` with `shape="circle"` and
`raised`. There is no `helix-fab` here, and the reason is worth stating,
because a component would have re-declared `appearance`, `tone`, `label` and
a size around a control that already has all four. A round raised button is a
shape, and where it sits is `data-dock` in the base layer.

horizontal pair for going in and coming back; a dial goes nowhere, so all four
arrows move through the actions and a reader who guesses either axis is
answered. That is the controller's own house position, and this is a component
with no reason to argue with it.

members.name: announce
members.description:
Tells a slotted trigger what it is doing, since it cannot know.

The fallback button is rendered by this element and says so in its own
template. A trigger the consumer slotted is their markup, and the state it
needs to announce is state only this element holds: without this, the
arrangement this component recommends, an icon button slotted as the
trigger, is a control that opens a menu and never says it has one.

Written onto their element rather than asked of them, because a consumer who
has to mirror `open` back onto their own trigger is a consumer who will
forget, and the failure is silent to everyone who can see the screen.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.summary: A button that fans out the few actions a screen is for.

declarations.description:
**One axis, and nesting is how you get two.** The sandbox this was taken from
moves a cross: a divider down the middle, another across the bottom, and a
corner that moves both. That is a layout rather than a component, and every
part of it that is worth sharing is one divider between two panes. A splitter
inside a splitter gives the cross back, and gives the three-pane and the
four-pane arrangements it never had.

**Where two of them cross there is a corner, and it moves both.** A splitter
slotted into a pane of another, at right angles to it, has one end of its
divider sitting exactly on the other's. That end grows a handle: `move` under
the pointer, both arrow axes on the keyboard, and a drag that carries the two
positions at once.

**The outer splitter draws it and the nested one announces itself upward.**
Built the other way round first, because a splitter already knows where its
own divider begins and needs no measurement of the other, and that version was
clipped: the crossing lies on the boundary between a pane and the divider
beside it, a handle centered there reaches back over the boundary, and a pane
is `overflow: auto`. Exactly half the corner was cut off. The outer separator
is the one element that already straddles the seam, so the corner belongs in
it.

That makes the channel between the two a single call in a single direction:
`cross(child, at)` says where the child crosses, `moveTo` drives either one,
and neither reads the other's state. The child is what calls it, because a
parent cannot poll for a child that has not upgraded yet.

The one number it carries is a percentage rather than a measurement, which is
what keeps either of them from measuring the other, and it assumes the nested
splitter fills its pane. That is what slotting one into a pane does. Give the
nested splitter its own inset, or wrap it in something smaller than the pane,
and the corner is drawn where the crossing would be rather than where it is.

**It is a client-side enhancement and says so.** Finding the parent means
inspecting the tree, which a server cannot do, so the corner appears at
`firstUpdated` and never in the served markup. That is allowed for exactly
this: it is an affordance rather than content, and a splitter with no corner
yet is a splitter with two working dividers.

Where two dividers are parallel there is no corner, because there is nothing
to take hold of. Where they cross without a corner, the inner divider takes
the pointer: every separator sits on the same layer, so a tie goes to document
order and a deeper splitter is always later.

**A divider that is moving says so, whoever is moving it.** `:hover` cannot
carry that: a drag holds the pointer through capture and a fast one leaves the
target behind, and a corner moves the nested divider while the reader is on
the crossing, nowhere near it. So a drag in progress is a state, and both
dividers a corner moves are lit for as long as it moves them.

**The divider is a real `role="separator"` with `aria-valuenow`, moved by the
arrow keys as well as by pointer.** A divider only a mouse can move is
unusable without one, which is the reason the sandbox's carries the same, and
`Home` and `End` take it to its bounds.

**It goes where it is put, all the way to either end.** `min` and `max` are
nothing and everything unless a consumer says otherwise, because a divider
that stops dead short of the edge gives a reader no way to put a pane away.
Where a pane should keep a sliver of itself, only whoever put the tabs on it
knows how much, so they say so.

**A pane can be shut, and that is not the same as a divider at the edge.**
The geometry is identical and the knowledge is not: only a shut pane knows
where to open back to. So `collapsed` is a second state rather than a reading
of the position, and the position it opens to is simply the one collapsing
never overwrote. `collapsed-size` keeps a sliver showing where a pane has a
tab strip worth leaving, and collapse overrides `min` and `max`, which is
what those are for: they keep a pane from vanishing by accident, and this is
the deliberate version.

The two are kept in step in one direction only: a drag that settles on the
collapsed size latches shut, and any move opens it again. Otherwise a reader
could drag a pane closed and the consumer's own button would still be
offering to close it.

A pane shut to nothing is told apart from one shut to a sliver, because the
two want different dividers: a sliver still has a boundary worth drawing, and
nothing leaves the divider sitting on the container's own edge.

**The box is measured once, when a drag starts.** Measuring per move is a
forced layout on every pointer event, in the middle of a gesture whose whole
job is to stay ahead of the pointer, and nothing about the box moves while the
divider does.

**`helix-change` fires when it settles, not while it moves.** A drag is a
stream of positions and only the one it ends at is a preference; announcing
each would ask a consumer to write to storage a hundred times to record one
decision. Nothing is stored here either: where a preference lives, and whether
it should be kept at all, is the consumer's to decide, and a component writing
to storage on its own would be deciding for all of them under a key it chose.

members.name: orientation
members.description:
Which way the panes are laid out.

`horizontal` is side by side with an upright divider between them, and
`aria-orientation` on that divider is therefore `vertical`: a separator's
orientation is the direction it is *drawn* in, not the axis it moves along,
so the two words are opposite each other here on purpose. The code had this
right and the sentence beside it said the reverse.

Unset is horizontal and stays unset, so a reflected default cannot appear on
a host whose server output never had it.

members.name: position
members.description:
Where the divider sits, as a percentage of the whole.

Reading gives where it is; writing declares it the consumer's, and
`default-position` seeds one this element owns. The same accessor pair
`Pagination.page` and the calendar's `month` carry.

members.name: defaultPosition
members.description: Where the divider starts, where nothing declared it.

members.name: collapsed
members.description:
Which pane is shut, if either.

The same accessor pair as `position`, and deliberately a second state
rather than a reading of the first. A pane shut by dragging the divider to
the edge and a pane shut on purpose look identical in geometry and are not
the same thing: only the second knows where to go back to. Kept apart, the
open position is simply the one collapsing never overwrote, so restoring
needs no memory of its own.

It overrides `min` and `max`, which is the point of it. Those keep a sliver
of a pane during a drag; this is the thing that says the sliver can go.

members.name: defaultCollapsed
members.description: Which pane starts shut, where nothing declared it.

members.name: collapsedSize
members.description:
How much of a shut pane is still shown, as a percentage.

Zero by default, which is a pane fully gone. A tab strip or a title bar
that should survive its own collapse says how much of itself to keep, and
only whoever put it there knows that, which is the same reason `min` is a
consumer's to set.

members.name: min
members.description: Nearest the divider may come to the start, as a percentage.

members.name: max
members.description: Nearest it may come to the end.

members.name: step
members.description: How far one arrow press moves it, as a percentage.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the divider.

members.name: cornerLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the handle where two dividers cross.

members.name: positionState
members.description: The position, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: positionMode
members.description: Whether the consumer owns it, decided once and then fixed.

members.name: collapsedState
members.description: The collapse, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: collapsedMode
members.description: Whether the consumer owns it, decided once and then fixed.

members.name: opened
members.description:
Where the divider was before the gesture that may be about to shut it.

A drag writes a position on every pointer move, so by the time it reaches
the edge the number it started from is gone. Taken once, on the press, and
written back if the gesture ends shut, so the pane opens to where it was
rather than to the edge it was dragged against.

members.name: reached
members.description:
Where the gesture has moved to, whether or not it was applied. See `move`.

`@state`, because the divider is drawn from it while a drag is under way.

members.name: showing
members.description:
The position to draw, which is not always the position to report.

A controlled splitter applies nothing, so `position` holds still for the
whole gesture and the divider stayed where it was until the pointer came up
and the consumer answered: it jumped to the end rather than following the
hand. Reported as resizing that was not seamless and did not work as it had.

So a drag draws itself. The number is not announced until it settles, which
is the rule that has not changed, and the consumer's answer takes over the
moment they give one. It is what the sandbox did for itself before it used
this component: write the size on every pointer move, tell anyone once.

members.name: dragging
members.description:
Whether this divider is being moved right now, by anything.

`:hover` is not enough on its own. A drag holds the pointer through capture
and a fast one leaves the eight pixel target behind, and a corner moves a
divider the pointer is nowhere near: the nested one, while the reader is on
the crossing. Both are dividers that are moving and should say so.

A `data-` attribute on an element in this shadow root, never on the host.

members.name: crossings
members.description:
Nested splitters that cross this one, and how far along they cross it.

Written by the child, not found by the parent: a parent cannot poll for a
child that has not upgraded, so the child announces itself once it has. The
number is the child's own `position`, which is also its offset along this
divider, because the child fills the pane and the pane spans this splitter
end to end on the axis the divider runs.

Not `@state`, because the array is mutated in place. `cross` and `uncross`
request the update themselves.

members.name: outer
members.description: The splitter this one is nested in, once it has found it.

members.name: crossedAt
members.description: The last position announced upward, so an unchanged one costs nothing.

members.name: cornerOrigin
members.description: The two boxes a corner drag is measured against, taken once.

members.name: origin
members.description:
The host's box, measured once when a drag starts.

Measuring per move is a forced layout on every pointer event, in the middle
of a gesture whose whole job is to stay ahead of the pointer. Nothing about
it moves while the divider does.

members.name: moveTo
members.description:
Moves the divider, and optionally says so.

Public because a corner on a nested splitter has to drive the one it is
nested in, and that is the whole of what it needs: the pair are not
otherwise coupled and neither reads the other's state. `settled` is false
for each step of a drag and true once, at the end, for the reason a drag
announces once: only the position it ends at is a preference.

members.name: sliver
members.description: The collapsed size, held inside the range a percentage can be.

members.name: flush
members.description:
Whether the divider is against an edge with nothing beside it.

Geometry, not state, which is the second answer here: it asked whether the
pane was `collapsed`, and a divider driven to the edge by a consumer setting
`position` is just as flush and drew a line anyway. What the stylesheet
needs to know is whether there is a pane on both sides, and that is a fact
about where the divider is however it got there.

Still not the same question as `collapsed`: a pane shut to a sliver has a
boundary worth drawing, and one shut to nothing has the container's own edge
there instead.

members.name: clamp
members.description: Pulled between the bounds, which are the ends unless a consumer moved them.

members.name: vertical
members.description: Public because a nested splitter compares axes with the one it is in.

members.name: move
members.description:
Asks to move, and applies it where the position is this element's to move.

Not announced per step: `helix-change` is the settling, below. A drag that
announced every position would be asking a consumer to record a hundred
decisions to keep one.

members.name: settle
members.description:
Says the arrangement has settled, so a consumer can keep it.

Through the audited path, so a consumer who owns `position` is told what was
asked for and decides, and one who does not has already had it applied.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
The keys a separator answers.

One axis, the one the divider actually travels along, plus `Home` and `End`
for its bounds. The other two arrows are left alone and the page scrolls
under them as it would anywhere else.

*Corrected 18 Aug 2026. This said "both axes, always", on the reasoning
`KeyboardNavigationController` uses for a set of items: a reader who guesses
the wrong arrow gets nothing. The code has never done it, and measuring the
three tab stops of a nested pair is what turned that up, so the prose was
describing a decision nobody implemented.*

*Leaving it as one axis, because nesting is what settles it. Taking all four
would mean `ArrowLeft` moving a horizontal divider up and down, which is not
a reader being helped past a guess, it is an arrow that does not go the way
it points. And the guess it was protecting against is answered better by the
corner: there, all four arrows are live and each moves the divider it points
along, which is the only place in a splitter where a second axis means
anything.*

members.name: reset
members.description: Puts the divider back where the markup put it.

members.name: handleCornerDoubleClick
members.description:
Both of them, because the corner moves both.

It needs its own handler now. Inside the separator this came free by
bubbling, and moving the corner out to sit against the host for the stacking
reason took the double click with it: the divider reset and the crossing
did not. Reported.

members.name: cross
members.description:
Records that a nested splitter crosses this one at `at` percent along it.

Public because it is the whole of the channel between the two, and it runs
one way: the child tells the parent where it is, and the parent draws the
corner and drives them both. Nothing is read back, so neither has to know
anything about the other's state.

members.name: uncross
members.description: Forgets a nested splitter that has left the tree. See `cross`.

members.name: findOuter
members.description:
Announces this splitter to the one it is nested in, if they cross.

Client only. The server has no tree to walk, and a parent that has not
upgraded has no `orientation` to compare against, so this waits for
`firstUpdated`. That is what the corner is allowed to be: an affordance
rather than content, absent from the served markup and appearing at
hydration, with two working dividers in the meantime.

`parentElement` before `closest`, so a splitter does not find itself.

members.name: handleCornerMove
members.description: Both axes at once, each measured against the splitter that owns it.

members.name: handleCornerKeydown
members.description:
The corner takes every arrow, each moving the splitter whose axis it points
along, which is the only reading a keyboard can give a handle that moves in
two directions.

members.name: leaveSeparator
members.description:

not depend on where the element happens to sit, and `preventDefault` is
still needed either way: a drag across a pane would otherwise select the
text under it.

declarations.summary: One measurement, with the word for what it measures.

declarations.description:
**`active` names where the reader is. `complete` stays on each step.** They
are two different facts and only one of them is positional. Deriving both
from a position is the obvious design and it is wrong the first time anybody
steps back: return to stage one of three and stages one and two are still
finished, while "everything before the active one" says only the first is.
So this element drives `current` and never touches `complete`.

**`active` is optional, and a sequence without it still renders.** Left
unset, each step's own `current` stands and nothing here overwrites it, which
is what lets the whole sequence be right in the server's markup: this element
would have to count its slotted children to know which one is third, and the
server has no children to count. Set it, and it wins, because it is a
statement about the sequence where the attribute on a step is a statement
about one step.

That is also why the numbering is not JavaScript. It is a CSS counter in the
tier above, which the browser resolves at layout with no script at all, so
the third step reads "3" in the server's own markup.

**The connector belongs to the step, not to the list.** Each one draws the
line that arrives at it and hides it when it is first, the same arrangement
Breadcrumbs uses for its separator and for the same reason: a line drawn
between items needs either an index or a parent that counts, and drawing it
on the item needs neither.

`role="list"` on the host rather than an `<ol>` in the shadow root. The steps
are the consumer's elements in the light DOM, so an `<ol>` here would be a
list whose items are somewhere else.

members.name: label
members.description:
Accessible name for the sequence.

A list of stages is a landmark a reader arrives at out of order, so it
needs a name of its own rather than borrowing the heading above it.

members.name: orientation
members.description:
Which way the steps run.

Absent is a row, which is what a form header wants, with each name under
its mark: beside them there is a word in the rule's path and the line would
be struck through it. `vertical` stacks them, names beside their marks,
which is the shape with room under a step for what the stage holds.

Each axis has one arrangement rather than a second property offering both
in both. Of those four combinations three are ones nobody should pick, and
a property whose job is mostly to be left alone is a property that mostly
catches people out.

members.name: appearance
members.description:
What each step is marked with.

Absent is the state itself: a check where a stage is done, a target where
the reader is, an empty ring ahead of them. Three marks that need no
legend, which a number does: "3" says where a stage sits in the order and
nothing about whether it is finished.

`numeric` is the older convention and is still the right one where the
order is the point, a form that says "step 3 of 5" beside it, or a sequence
a reader is told to come back to by number.

members.name: steps

members.name: sync
members.description:

Returns without touching anything where nothing has set `active`, which is
the case a server renders: the steps' own `current` is the state then, and
overwriting it on hydration is exactly the flash this design exists to
avoid.

`current` only. `complete` is the consumer's on each step, because a reader
who steps back has finished more stages than they are standing in front of.

members.name: active
members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Called `active`, which is what this mixin is named for and what it was
not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

members.name: defaultActive
members.description: Initial item for uncontrolled use. Ignored once `active` is written.

members.name: activeState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: activeMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `active` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: requestActive
members.description:
Requests a new current item, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Unlike a native control, nothing has moved
by the time this runs, so refusing is simply not writing: there is
nothing to put back.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:
Which item is current, given what there is to choose from.

The first enabled one when `value` names nothing, which is a set before
its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

declarations.summary: A sequence of stages, and where the reader is in it.

declarations.description:
**The name is a button, and only the name.** A stepper is something a reader
goes back through, and the thing they reach for is the name of the stage. The
marker is `aria-hidden` decoration, so wrapping it in the button would add
hit area and no meaning: the accessible name would be the text either way,
and what is pressable would stop being the same shape as what is readable.

It is `helix-button`, not a `<button>` this element resets and dresses. The
hover wash, the focus ring, the disabled treatment and the way the label sits
against an icon are all decisions the button already carries, and a second
copy of them here is a second copy to keep in step. `ghost` is the quiet
shape: transparent until it is pointed at.

It says nothing about where a reader may go. Every step is pressable and
announces itself with `helix-select`; refusing the ones ahead is `disabled`,
which the consumer sets because only the consumer knows whether a form can be
skipped. A component that guessed would be wrong on the first wizard that
lets you jump to the end.

**The marker is a slot whose fallback is the state.** A finished stage shows
a check, the current one a target, and one not yet reached an empty ring:
three marks that say what a reader wants to know without a legend. A consumer
who wants their own fills the slot instead.

The step renders exactly one of the three, chosen from its own two booleans.
Rendering all three and hiding two in CSS would work and is worse: the
accessibility tree would carry marks that are not there, and the markup would
say three things about a stage that is one.

Numbering is a separate question and belongs to the tier above. `numeric`
hides the mark and shows a CSS counter, which the browser resolves at layout,
so the digit costs no script and is right in the server's markup however the
steps are ordered. Nothing here knows which appearance is in use, and does
not need to.

**`complete` and `current` are separate, and both can be false.** A stage
that is neither is one the reader has not reached, which is the majority of
any sequence and therefore the state that needs no attribute. They can also
both be true: a reader who steps back into a finished stage is in it and has
finished it, and a stepper that forgets the second is one that loses its
checks the moment somebody reviews their answers.

**The `content` slot opens on the current step, and only down a column.** A
row has no room under a step to put a form in, and stretching one to fit
would set every step's height by the tallest. `current` is what opens it, so
the state that says where the reader is is also the state that shows them the
stage: one attribute, no second flag to keep in step with it, and it renders
open on the server rather than after hydration.

members.name: mark
members.description:
The mark this stage's state calls for.

`complete` first, so a stage a reader has stepped back into keeps its check
rather than losing it to the target: they did finish it, and the name and
the rule below still say which one is open.

**Three shapes, and the reader can tell them apart with the colour off.**
An outline circle for a stage nobody has reached, the same circle with a
centre for the one they are standing on, a bare check for one that is done.
The first two are one shape filling in, which is the progression, and the
check is the only mark that leaves the family because finishing is the only
state that is not a position in the sequence.

What went was the coin around the check: a filled disc carrying a check
beside a filled disc carrying a ring put two of the three inside the same
container, and left hue doing most of the work of telling them apart.

The bare check is `Timeline`'s, deliberately: the two components report the
same kind of thing, a sequence with marks down it, and a check floating on
a hairline in one beside a check inside a green coin in the other was two
answers to one question. Timeline's rings came off the same day.

declarations.summary: One stage in a sequence.

declarations.description:
**A switch is not a checkbox with a different shape.** A checkbox is an
answer to a question the form asks when it is submitted; a switch is a thing
happening now. That is why `role="switch"` exists and why a switch belongs
outside a form as often as in one: it says "on" and "off" rather than
"ticked" and "unticked", and a reader expects the effect immediately rather
than on Save.

Rendered as a real `<input type="checkbox">` carrying `role="switch"`, which
is the pairing ARIA describes: the input is what a form submits and what a
label forwards a press to, and the role is what a screen reader announces.
Neither half can be got from the other.

The label sits beside it, inside the `<label>` that forwards the press, the
way a checkbox's does. The hint and the message go under the row, because
there is no above: the switch and the words naming it are one line.

members.description:
Says on the `label` region whether anything is in it.

An empty region is not free: it is still a flex item, so it still takes the
container's gap. There is no selector that can ask, `slot:empty` being
about a slot's fallback rather than its assigned nodes, so the component
asks and says so, on the region inside this shadow root rather than on the
host: an attribute written onto the host is a change to markup the consumer
rendered, which React reports on hydration and does not patch up.

members.name: checked
members.description:
Whether the control is checked.

One property rather than two. Reading gives the real state whichever
mode the control is in; writing hands ownership to the consumer, which
is what the attribute in `<helix-checkbox checked>` does as well. The
same shape all four of these mixins have, for the reason given on
`MixinControllerOpen.open`.

Not reflected: the attribute is the consumer's input and stays as they
wrote it, and `data-checked` carries the resolved state for stylesheets.

members.name: defaultChecked
members.description: Initial checked state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: checkedState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: checkedMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `checked` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: requestChecked
members.description:
Requests a checked change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the
`helix-change` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode
the element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing
and waits for the consumer to pass a new `checked`, which is what
"controlled" means.

members.name: toggleChecked
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the control when the browser brings a form back.

Hand-written on the checkbox and nowhere else, so `Switch`, the mixin's
only other consumer, had no restore at all: a reader who navigated away
and came back to a restored form found their switch flipped off. The
mixin owns `checked`, so the mixin owns putting it back.

Through `checked` rather than the private state, so a controlled consumer
is asked the same way every other change asks.

members.name: resetChecked
members.description:
Drops the uncontrolled state, so the control reads `defaultChecked`
again.

A form reset has to return a control to what its markup declared, and
clearing `checked` alone only leaves controlled mode. The value the
element has been keeping lives here, so this is where it is dropped.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: formAssociated

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it

reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.summary: One cell of a table.

declarations.description:
A column is a heading and a width, declared together, because they are two
facts about one thing and keeping them apart is what went wrong before.

**This replaces a `columns` string on the table.** That property took a CSS
track list, so the headings lived in a row of cells and the widths lived in
an attribute, and nothing tied the two together: a table with three headings
and a two-track list rendered without complaint. Worse, handing it the
headings instead of a track list produced invalid CSS, which the grid
silently ignored, so the whole table collapsed into one column and every cell
stacked. That happened, in this library's own example, and the failure said
nothing at all.

Now the column is the source of both. Add one and the table has another
track; remove one and it does not.

**It generates no box of its own**, the same as a row: the heading is a grid
item of the table, so it lines up with the cells under it rather than sitting
in a wrapper that has to be kept the same width.

cssParts.description: The heading cell.
cssParts.name: column

members.name: width
members.description:
The track this column takes, as CSS.

A single track value, so anything valid in `grid-template-columns` works:
`16rem`, `auto`, `minmax(0, 2fr)`. Left unset the column shares what is
left over equally, which is `minmax(0, 1fr)` rather than `1fr`: a bare
`1fr` track keeps an automatic minimum and refuses to shrink under a long
cell, so one unbreakable value pushes the table past its container.

declarations.description:
A grid rather than a `<table>`, so every column lines up across rows while
each row stays a real element that can be styled, hidden, or made
interactive. Table layout gives column alignment and takes away almost
everything else; grid gives both.

The cost is that the roles have to be declared, since a grid of divs is not a
table to anyone reading it. `table`, `row`, `cell`, and `columnheader` are
all set explicitly, and rows are `display: contents` so their cells become
items of the one grid that does the aligning.

moment it has one. A raw track list is the right shape for the value and
the wrong place for it: the headings and the widths were two halves of one
fact held in two places, and nothing checked that they agreed. Worse, the
value is CSS, so handing it headings by mistake produced an invalid track

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description:
Nothing is assigned by name, so the columns can be put in a row.

`role="columnheader"` was landing directly under `role="table"` with no
owning `row`, which is invalid: the table pattern is `table > row >
columnheader`, and a header cell with no row is a cell belonging to
nothing. The columns are ordinary children the consumer writes with no
`slot`, so the only way to put a wrapper around them without changing what
a consumer writes is to assign them here.

consumer's own markup, which is the change a React consumer's hydration
reports and does not patch up. Assignment writes nothing at all.

the shadow root exists only after upgrade, and the assignment below runs in
that same update. There is no window in which the shadow is present and the
assignment has not happened.

members.name: appearance
members.description:
How the row reads.

Unset is a raised pill on the selected tab with nothing behind the row,
which is what a set sitting inside other chrome wants. `underlined` is a
rule under the row and a thicker one under the selected tab, for a set that
heads a page. `segmented` puts the pill in a framed, sunken track, which
reads as one control rather than as a row.

`segmented` and not `toggle`, which is what this was called. An appearance
value that is another component's name says "it looks like that one", which
a reader can only act on if they already know what that one looks like, and
every other appearance in the library describes itself: `outlined`,
`spaced`, `plain`. This component's own comments called it segmented in
both places it explained itself, which is the name that was doing the work.

`underlined` and not `underline` for the shape of the word rather than the
sense: the two values sit in one list and read as a pair, and `segmented`
is a participle. `outlined` on Accordion is the same word doing the same
job. The example file was already `underlined.html`, which is what a reader
meets first.

Reflected and left unset by default, so the host carries nothing a
consumer's server markup does not already have.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the tab list.

members.name: manual
members.description:
Whether arrowing to a tab also selects it.

Automatic is the default because showing a panel is usually cheap. Set this
where it is not, so a reader arrowing past four tabs does not load four
panels on the way.

members.name: observer
members.description: Watches for anything that moves a tab, since none of it is a property.

members.name: sync
members.description: Pushes the current value down to whichever tab and panel own it.

members.name: watch
members.description:
Watches every tab for a change of size.

Called again whenever the set changes, because `tabs` reads `this.children`
and filters on `instanceof`, so it is empty until the tab elements upgrade.
At `firstUpdated` it frequently is empty, and observing nothing is silent.

`observe` is idempotent per element, so re-running this costs nothing and
needs no bookkeeping about which tabs are already watched.

members.name: handleSlotChange
members.description:
The set changed: pair it up, watch it, and measure it.

All three, where this used to be `sync()` alone, and the missing `place()`
is why an indicator could stay unplaced for the life of the page. The order
of events is what does it: the host renders and measures before its tabs
have upgraded, so there is no selected tab to measure and `place` refuses;
the ResizeObserver's one initial callback lands in that same gap; and then
the tabs upgrade, `slotchange` pairs them, nothing measures, and nothing
ever will again, because the host's size never changes.

Invisible in every example, because a tab strip that is only tabs is
exactly as tall as its tabs, so a mark at the top of the strip is a mark on
the tab. It showed up where something gives the strip a height of its own.

members.name: active
members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Called `active`, which is what this mixin is named for and what it was
not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

members.name: defaultActive
members.description: Initial item for uncontrolled use. Ignored once `active` is written.

members.name: activeState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: activeMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `active` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: requestActive
members.description:
Requests a new current item, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Unlike a native control, nothing has moved
by the time this runs, so refusing is simply not writing: there is
nothing to put back.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:
Which item is current, given what there is to choose from.

The first enabled one when `value` names nothing, which is a set before
its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

so nothing here needs a guard.

declarations.description:
A real `<textarea>`, so the caret, the selection, spellcheck, the resize
handle and the keyboard a phone chooses are all the platform's, and it
serializes into the server's markup so the field is usable before any script
loads.

**Not an Input with a taller box.** The difference is the Enter key: in a
single-line field it submits the form, and here it inserts a line. That is a
behavioral difference the platform owns and cannot be styled into existence,
which is why this is its own element rather than `Input` with a property.

`rows` sets the height it starts at, and `auto-grow` lets it follow its own
content. They are not alternatives: `rows` is where an empty field begins and
`auto-grow` is what happens after, so a field that grows still has to start
somewhere.
