declarations.description:
**The region is why this is one family rather than two.** A live region has
to be in the document *before* a message is put into it: assistive technology
subscribes to the region, and a region that arrives already holding its
message is frequently not announced at all. So the container is a part of the
family and not an arranger of complete things, which is the same reasoning
that puts `Radio.Group` inside its own family.

**Polite, never assertive.** `role="alert"` interrupts whatever a reader is
being told, and almost nothing that arrives in a corner of the screen has
earned that. Something that genuinely cannot wait is a `Dialog`, which stops
the page for everyone rather than only for the people who cannot see it.

**It never creates or destroys anything.** The consumer renders items and
removes them; asking to go is a cancelable `helix-dismiss` from the item.
That is still exactly true of the region: an item that has gone hides itself
and stays in the tree, so a consumer whose state still lists it does not have
their framework fighting a node this component took away. What changed is
that the item no longer waits to be told before hiding, unless the consumer
declared `open` and said the state is theirs.
There is no `toast.show()`, because an imperative queue inside a component is
a second copy of the application's state that nothing can render from: an app
that wants a `toast()` function writes a thin one over the state it already
has, and keeps the ability to render the same messages on the server, in a
test, or twice.

declarations.description:
The indicator is one element that travels, not a background that appears on
whichever item is current. That difference is the whole point: a fill that
swaps is two things changing at once and reads as a flicker, while one that
moves is a single object the eye follows, and it says where the selection
came from as well as where it went.

Its whole box is measured from the selected item and written onto
the indicator as custom properties, because labels are different lengths and
no proportion of the group is the right answer. Measurement is client-side by
necessity, so the server renders the indicator hidden and it fades in once it
has somewhere to be, which is the harmless direction: it appears rather than
jumping from a wrong place.

A radio group, and only that. Navigation is links marked with `aria-current`
and styled by the `data-navigation-item` recipe: radio semantics would announce a
set of destinations as a set of choices. A tab controls a panel.

Being a radio group, it is a form control, and it says so through
`HelixFormElement`: it reports its value under a `name`, comes back to the
markup's choice on reset, and restores the one a reader made when the browser
brings a form back.

The semantics were already right: the host has carried `role="radiogroup"`
and the items `role="radio"` from the start. What none of it did was reach a
form. A button in a shadow root submits nothing whatever its role, so the
value has to be reported by the host, which is the only thing a form can
see.

They were one method because the geometry needed the active item anyway,
and that made a selection change look like a layout concern. `resolveActiveItem`
rather than the first item, because a group opening on a disabled segment
marked it as chosen.

members.name: watch
members.description:
Watches the group and every item it currently holds.

Called again on `slotchange`, because the set was read once at first paint:
an item added later was measured by nothing, so a group whose options
arrive with the data had a thumb that stopped following the moment one of
them changed width. Observing the same element twice is a no-op, so there
is nothing to unwind first.

members.name: validate
members.description:
The verdict on the answer, which `required` had been asking for and not
getting.

`required` arrived with `MixinField` and nothing enforced it: the attribute
reflected, the marker rendered beside the label, and a form with an
unanswered group submitted anyway. An API that exists and does nothing is
worse than one that is missing, because the marker is a promise to the
reader that something will stop them.

The anchor is the track rather than the host, so the browser's own bubble
points at the control rather than at a box with nothing in it.

members.name: labelPlacement
members.description:
Where the group's label sits, `start` putting it on the track's line.

Absent is above, which is what a field looks like and what almost every
group wants. `start` is for a row of controls that are labelled rather than
a form of fields: a toolbar reads as one line, and a label stacked over
every group in it turns one row into two.

**A placement rather than a slot, and that is the whole point of it.** A
`start` slot would let a consumer put the word there, and would also let
them put it there *instead of* setting `label`, which is the group's
accessible name: the set would then be named for nobody using a screen
reader while looking correct to everybody else. Worse, setting both draws
it twice. One property moves the label the consumer already has to give,
and cannot be used to remove it.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: controls
members.description:
Focusable controls, in document order.

Asks each child for its own focus target rather than matching tag names, so
a toolbar holds anything, including elements this package has never heard
of. Client only: there is no tree to walk on the server.

members.name: setTabStop
members.description:
Moves the single tab stop to one control.

Prefers the control's own `focusable` property to writing `tabindex` on it.
The attribute is a change to markup the consumer rendered, which a React
consumer's hydration reports and does not patch up; a control that offers
the property moves the stop inside its own shadow root instead.

`tabindex` stays as the fallback, because a toolbar has to hold controls
this package has never heard of.

members.name: claimTabStop
members.description:
Sets the first tab stop once every custom control has upgraded.

A custom element has no properties at all before it upgrades, so a pass
that ran first would find no `focusable`, take the `tabindex` fallback, and
write the very attribute this exists to avoid.

members.name: restoreTabStop
members.description:
Gives the tab stop back to a control that still exists.

`controls` excludes anything disabled or hidden, so disabling the control
holding the stop dropped it out of the list while every other control was
already at `-1`. The toolbar then had no tab stop at all and the keyboard
could not reach it again, from a change as ordinary as a Save button
disabling itself once the form is clean.

`foreign` stays false, the same as the first claim: a control this package
has never heard of that was never given `tabindex="-1"` is still in the
document's own tab order, so it is never the one that gets stranded.

members.name: axis
members.description:
The orientation in force.

Unset is horizontal, and stays unset: the default is the absent attribute,
so a reflected default cannot appear on the host after hydration.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.summary: A group of controls that share one tab stop.

declarations.description:
The trigger is slotted and stays the consumer's own element. The bubble is
rendered here, in the top layer through the popover API, so it clears any
ancestor with `overflow: hidden` without a `z-index` anywhere.

Position comes from `FloatingController`, which flips to another side when
the preferred one does not fit and slides along it to stay in view.

**Two forms, and they are not equivalent for a screen reader.**

Wrapping is the convenience form and is right where the bubble decorates a
control that already says what it is. The trigger stays the consumer's own
element, slotted, and nothing here can describe it: an IDREF cannot cross a
shadow boundary, an element reference is valid only into the same tree or a
shadow-including *ancestor* (the bubble's tree is neither, it is inward), and
a string on the trigger means writing to markup the consumer server-rendered.
All three measured.

`for` is the form that works. The tooltip sits *beside* the trigger in the
consumer's own tree and names it by id, so both are in one tree and an IDREF
between them is legal in the ordinary way:

```html
<helix-button id="save" aria-describedby="save-tip">Save</helix-button>
<helix-tooltip id="save-tip" for="save" content="Save your work"></helix-tooltip>
```

Note that the reference points at *this host*, not at the bubble inside its
shadow root: the description is computed from the flat tree, which descends
into shadow content on its own.

**The consumer writes that `aria-describedby`, and nothing here writes it for
them.** WebAwesome and Spectrum Web Components both do write it, with
`setAttribute` on the trigger at runtime, which is the one thing this library
declines everywhere: React rendered that element on the server without the
attribute and reports a mismatch it will not patch up. Two ids in the markup
is the whole cost of the version that is correct before any JavaScript runs.

Because it is the consumer's line to write, it is also theirs to forget, so
`for` audits itself on first open and says so once. Same shape as
`requestControlledChange` warning about a controlled property nothing
answered.

It shows on hover and on focus, and hides on leave, on blur, on Escape, and
once the trigger has been activated: the hint is spent when the control has
been used.
A tooltip that answers only the pointer is one a keyboard reader never sees.

The pointer waits out `delay` first, or sweeping a row of controls flashes a
tooltip for each of them. Focus does not wait: a keyboard reader landing on a
control has already committed to it.

Open state comes from `MixinControllerOpen`, so it announces `helix-open` and
`helix-close` like every other overlay here, and a consumer can drive it with
`open` where they need to.

cssParts.description: The bubble.

slots.description: The bubble's content, when `content` is not enough. Anything slotted here replaces the property, which is this slot's fallback.
slots.name: content

members.name: content
members.description:
The text shown in the bubble.

The common case, and the fallback for the `content` slot: slot something
there and it replaces this. Both cannot show at once, which is the point
of using fallback content rather than rendering whichever is present.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of the element this describes, in this tooltip's own tree.

Set it and the tooltip stops wrapping: it renders no trigger, listens on
the element it names, and points its bubble there. Leave it unset and the
default slot is the trigger, which is the older form.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a tooltip inside another component's
shadow root names an element in that root rather than in the document.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, which is
worth knowing before someone reads the DOM and thinks it did not take.
Measured against React 19.2.8: `for` exists on the prototype, so React sets
`element.for = 'save'` and writes nothing to the markup, where `content`
and `placement`, which are not properties on the class at that moment, come
through as attributes. Both paths reach the same place through Lit, so
nothing is broken by it; a `[for]` selector would find nothing, which is
why this does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: placement
members.description: Preferred side. It moves if that side does not fit.

members.name: offset
members.description:
Space between the trigger and the bubble, in pixels.

Eight, which used to be the size of the arrow the styled tier drew so the
point could reach the trigger while the bubble did not. **The arrow is
gone**, and the number stays: it is now simply the gap, and eight is what
reads as beside rather than attached at every placement. Nothing depends on
it any more, so a consumer changing it changes the gap and nothing else.

members.name: disabled
members.description: Whether the tooltip never shows.

members.name: delay
members.description:
How long the pointer must rest before the bubble appears, in milliseconds.

Without one, sweeping across a row of controls flashes a tooltip for each
of them, which is noise rather than help. Focus opens with no delay: a
keyboard reader arriving on a control has already committed to it.

members.name: delayOut
members.description: How long the bubble stays after the pointer leaves, in milliseconds.

members.name: holds
members.description:
What is currently keeping the bubble up.

The pointer and focus are two holders and they shared one timer with
nothing counting them, so whichever left last won: moving the pointer off a
control that still had keyboard focus scheduled a hide and took the bubble
away from under the reader. The same fault the toast timer had, and the
same answer.

members.name: trigger
members.description:
The element the bubble points at.

The trigger, not the host. The host is `display: contents` so it wraps
without adding a box, and an element that generates no box measures as
nothing at the document origin: the bubble was placed against the corner
of the viewport rather than against the button.

members.name: named
members.description:
The element `for` names, or null.

`getRootNode()` rather than `document`, which is what makes this work inside
another component: an id is unique to a tree, and a tooltip in a shadow root
names an element in that root. Client only, since the server has no tree to
search.

members.name: bubbleLayer
members.default: new PopoverController(this, { anchor: () => this.trigger, /* Annotated, because without it the array's element type is inferred from `this`, whose own type depends on this controller, and TypeScript stops at the cycle. */ boundary: (): readonly (Element | null)[] => [this, this.named], offset: () => this.offset, onDismiss: () => this.hide(), placement: () => this.placement, surface: () => this.renderRoot.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="tooltip"]'), })

members.name: hasContent
members.description: Whether there is anything to show. Asked of the slot rather than of the property, because either can carry the content. `assignedNodes` without `flatten` answers what the consumer provided and not what the fallback would render, which is exactly the question: a bubble with only fallback and an empty property is empty. Text or an element, because neither alone is the test. An element on its own would count ` ` as something to say, and text on its own would count an icon as nothing, when an icon is the whole point of slotting rather than setting the property. Client only. The server has no assignment to inspect, and nothing calls this there: a tooltip opens in response to a pointer or to focus.

members.name: describedText
members.description:
The bubble's words as a plain string, for naming the host.

The property when it is set, otherwise whatever was slotted, flattened.
Rich content collapses to its text, which is the right answer for a
description: `Save ⌘ S` is what a reader needs, not the markup.

members.name: handleContentChange
members.description:
Re-links the description when what is in the bubble changes.

`updated` alone is not enough: content arriving from the light DOM changes
no property here, so nothing would schedule the update that re-reads it. A
consumer rendering the bubble's content after this upgrades, which is what
a framework does, would leave the trigger describing nothing.

members.name: show
members.description: Shows the bubble, unless there is nothing to show.

members.name: hide
members.description: Hides the bubble.

members.name: showLater
members.description: Shows after the pointer has rested for `delay`.

members.name: hideLater
members.description: Hides after `delayOut`, so crossing the gap to the bubble does not close it.

members.name: release
members.description: Hides only once nothing is holding the bubble up.

members.name: handleActivate
members.description:
Activating the trigger closes the bubble, which nothing was doing.

A tooltip is a hint about what a control will do, and once the control has
been used the hint is spent. Nothing else was going to take it down either:
`pointerleave` cannot fire while the pointer is still on the button it just
pressed, and `focusout` does not fire when activation leaves focus where it
was. So a gear that opened a drawer left its own label floating over the
drawer until the reader moved the mouse away.

`click` rather than `pointerdown`, because it is the one event both a mouse
and a keyboard produce: Enter and Space on a focused button raise it, and a
hint that outlived activation for keyboard readers alone would be the same
bug with a smaller audience.

Holds are cleared as well as hiding, the same as Escape. Leaving them set
means the pointer is still recorded as being over the trigger, so the next
`focusout` anywhere releases nothing and the bubble comes back on a
`release` it should have been dropped from.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
Escape closes the bubble from wherever the reader is.

On the document, not on the host, which is where it was: a tooltip opened
by hover has focus somewhere else entirely, so the press never reached this
element and Escape worked only for the one case that needed it least. That
is the case the pattern names, a reader escaping a tooltip obscuring what
is under it, and it was the case that did nothing.

Not stopped from propagating: a tooltip is not what the reader was trying
to escape if it sits inside something else that also closes.

members.name: bound
members.description:
What the pointer and focus listeners are currently on.

Held, rather than recomputed at removal time, because what `for` names can
change: unbinding from wherever the element is *now* leaves a live listener
on wherever it was, and a tooltip that opens from a control it no longer
describes is worse than one that does not open at all.

members.name: bind
members.description:
Puts the listeners on whatever the trigger is.

The host when it wraps, since the trigger is inside it and both `focusin`
and `focusout` bubble. The named element when `for` is set, because then the
host wraps nothing and `pointerenter` does not bubble at all.

Client only, and after the first render: `for` names an element that may not
have upgraded, or existed, when this one connected.

members.name: audited
members.description: Said once per element, however many times it opens.

members.name: auditDescription
members.description:
Checks that the trigger actually points back, and says so once if not.

`for` is only half a link: this element finds the trigger, and the trigger
has to name this element for a screen reader to read the two together. That
second half is the consumer's line to write, deliberately, because writing
it from here means `setAttribute` on markup they server-rendered. So it is
theirs to forget, and a silent accessibility gap is the worst kind: the
tooltip looks completely correct.

On first open rather than on connect, because a framework may render the
attribute after this element upgrades, and because a tooltip that never
opens has described nothing eitherway.

Either attribute counts. WebAwesome uses `aria-labelledby` over
`aria-describedby` on purpose, their reasoning being that some screen
readers want the description on the focusable element itself while a label
reads on first focus regardless, and that is a live enough question that
this should not be the thing to settle it.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`

declarations.summary: A short description that appears beside what it describes.

declarations.description:
The root owns the order and nothing else. Which stop is current, what Next
and Back mean, when the run is finished; the stops own where they point, and
the consumer owns every word.

**The spotlight is a shadow, not a hole.** The scrim is a box the size of the
current target with an enormous spread on its `box-shadow`, so the darkness
is what the shadow paints and the target is simply where the box is. A
`clip-path` on a full-screen scrim is the other way to do it and is worse
here: it needs the viewport in the same coordinate space as the cut, which
stops being true the moment anything between them is transformed.

**It measures, and this is a case where measuring is the only option.** The
target is an element somewhere else on the page whose position nothing can
know statically. That is different from a trail folding by width, where the
design rule was expressible and the measurement was answering a question
nobody had asked. Here the question is "where is that button", and there is
no other way to ask it.

**Nothing is measured on the server and nothing needs to be.** A tour starts
closed and a closed tour draws nothing, so the server renders the stops as
inert markup and the first frame is correct. This is also what makes it
acceptable for the root to write `current` onto stops it does not own: there
is no server state for the write to disagree with.

**It cannot point inside a modal, and nothing can fix that here.**
`showModal()` makes everything outside the dialog's own subtree inert, so a
panel anywhere else is unpressable however the top layer is ordered: this is
what modal means rather than a stacking accident. Measured with a modal
`Drawer` open, `elementsFromPoint` over the tour's own Done button returned
the drawer, the press light-dismissed the drawer, and the tour heard nothing
at all. Anything a tour points into has to stay reachable, which for `Drawer`
and `Dialog` means not modal while the tour is running.

**Focus is not trapped.** A reader has to be able to look at, and reach, the
thing being pointed at. `Escape` leaves, which is the one binding a tour
needs and the one every reader already tries.

declarations.summary: A guided run through an interface, one stop at a time.

declarations.description:
A stop names a target with `for` and holds whatever the consumer puts in it.
It owns no content of its own, which is the whole shape of this family: the
tour abstracts the three things that are genuinely hard, and the words are
the consumer's.

What it does own:

- **Where the panel goes.** Anchored to the target through the same floating
  pass every other overlay here uses.
- **That it is on top.** A popover, so it is in the top layer. A tour points
  at things inside dialogs, inside scrollers, inside anything with a stacking
  context, and a panel in the ordinary flow loses to all three.
- **When it shows.** Which is `current`, and which the root decides.

What it does not own is the heading, the paragraph, the picture and the
layout. Slot a `helix-card`, or a heading and a line of prose, or anything
else. This was written the other way first, with `title` and `body` parts and
a fixed arrangement, which is a component deciding what a tour is allowed to
say.

**The buttons are slot fallback, so the common case costs nothing and the
uncommon one is possible.** Write nothing and get Back, Next and Skip already
wired. Slot `actions` and they are yours, driven by `next()`, `back()` and
`skip()` on the root, which are public for exactly that.

**`for` is an id, the same as `Tooltip`'s.** The target is elsewhere on the
page, and an id is the one reference a consumer can write in markup without
holding an element. Resolved against the root node, so a stop inside a shadow
tree points at a target in that tree.

members.name: renderActions
members.description:
Skip, back and next, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

They are slot fallback rather than markup a consumer has to write, so a
tour with nothing slotted still has the three controls a tour needs; and
they are a method as well, so a tier above can render its own three without
reimplementing the panel around them. Both are needed: the slot is for the
consumer and the method is for the tier.

members.name: ask
members.description:
Says what the reader pressed and lets the root decide.

A stop cannot move a tour: it does not know what is after it, and a stop
that reached up to its parent to find out would be a stop that only works
inside one. Composed, so the root hears it through its own slot.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.description:
**`open`, on `MixinControllerOpen`, where it was a bare `expanded` boolean.**
A branch showing its children is the same state a disclosure holds, and
`AccordionItem` has been on that mixin all along. Written here by hand it had
neither half of what the mixin gives: `this.expanded = !this.expanded`
announced nothing, so a consumer could not know a branch had opened, and
could not own the state either. `aria-expanded` is still what the row
renders, because that is the attribute a tree uses; the property is what
changed, not the semantics.

An element rather than a slot because it owns state: whether it is open,
whether it is selected, and whether it is the one holding focus.

A branch is any item with something slotted into `children`, detected in
`firstUpdated` rather than declared by the consumer. That is a client-side
enhancement by necessity, since the server cannot inspect children, so the
server renders the node as a leaf and the twisty appears on hydration. It
appears rather than disappearing, which is the harmless direction.

members.description:

Which element that is moves with `href`: the thing carrying `treeitem` is
the thing the tree's roving tab stop lives on, and with a link that is the

members.name: select
members.description: Selects this node and announces it.

members.name: activate
members.description:
Chooses this node the way a reader does, from a press or from Enter.

Selecting and following are two things and this is where they meet, so the
pointer and the keyboard take one path to the same end. The tree calls this
rather than `select` for the keyboard, which is what fixes Enter: a nav
tree whose rows are links could be walked with the arrows and not entered,
because choosing announced a value and nothing listened for it.

members.name: follow
members.description:
Follows a link slotted into the name, if there is one.

A row is wider than the words in it: the indent, the padding, and with the
chevron at the far end most of the row's width are all outside the anchor,
so a reader who pressed the row anywhere but on the text got nothing. The
words are the consumer's own content and this does not rewrite them, so
what it does instead is press the link they put there.

The consumer's anchor rather than an `href` of this element's own,
deliberately: a framework's link component is what carries prefetching and
client-side routing, and a plain `<a href>` rendered in here would be a
full page load on a site that had neither. A synthetic click is what those
components listen for, so both keep working.

`querySelector` on the light DOM, not the render root: the link is the
consumer's, and it is scoped to this item's own name rather than to the
whole subtree, or a branch would follow the first link belonging to one of
its children.

members.name: renderRow
members.description: Everything inside the row, which is the same whichever element it is.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

declarations.summary: One node in a tree.

helix.documentation:
https://helix.fusion.dev/components/tree

**`href` makes the row itself the link.** A tree used as navigation is a list
of links, and the row is what a reader presses: with the anchor slotted into
the name instead, everything outside the words is dead, Enter does nothing,
and there is no middle-click, no status bar and no open-in-new-tab. Given an
`href` the row *is* an `<a>`, so the platform provides all of that and the
keyboard needs no handler at all.

It changes the shape of the ARIA, which is why it is a property and not the
default. An anchor cannot contain the group, since the group holds more
anchors and nesting them is invalid, so the row carries `treeitem` and the
group becomes its sibling under a presentational wrapper. That is exactly the
navigation flavour of the tree pattern, and the arrangement without an `href`
stays as it was: `treeitem` containing `group`, which is what an `<li>`
holding a `<ul>` is.

A consumer whose framework owns routing slots its own link instead and leaves
`href` unset. The row follows that one too, so the whole row works either
way; what the anchor adds is what only a real anchor can give.

declarations.description:
Focus is a single tab stop, moved with the arrow keys, which is what the tree
pattern requires: a sidebar of forty items should not be forty presses of Tab
to get past. The tree owns which item is the tab stop and moves it as focus
moves, so the browser's own focus order is never fought with.

Items are found with `instanceof`, never by tag name, so the headless tier
does not learn about the styled one.

cssParts.description: The tree container.
cssParts.name: tree

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the tree.

members.name: items
members.description:
Every item, in the order a reader moving down would meet them.

Selected by tag rather than by walking everything and filtering. `'*'` built
an array of every descendant element in the tree, labels and icons and
whatever a consumer slotted into a row included, and threw most of it away;
on a tree of any size that is the array a single arrow press rebuilds.

The two tag names rather than `instanceof` on everything: a styled
`helix-tree-item` extends the base, so both names are needed, and the
`instanceof` stays as the type guard because a consumer can write either
tag and neither selector proves what the element is.

members.name: visibleItems
members.description: Items a reader can actually reach: not inside a collapsed branch.

members.name: syncItems
members.description:
Pushes tree-owned state down: which item is selected, which holds the tab
stop, and how deep each one sits.

Depth is computed here rather than by each item counting its own ancestors,
so an item moved in the tree gets the right indent without knowing it moved.

members.name: handleBranch
members.description:
A branch opened or closed, whoever did it.

The keyboard paths called `syncItems` by hand and the pointer path did not,
so collapsing a branch by clicking its chevron left the tab stop on a row
inside the subtree that had just been hidden: the tree kept its one stop
and the stop was on something nobody could see or reach. Listening for the
item's own open events covers every way a branch can move, including a
consumer setting `open` directly.

Reflected, because a stylesheet needs it: the rows that are already there

members.name: loadingText
members.description: What is said while they are on their way.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: What is said where there are none, and none are coming.

members.name: countRows
members.description:

thing an empty state must never do. Listbox's spec caught precisely that.

members.name: renderStatus
members.description:
The status line, or nothing where there is content to show.

Loading wins over empty. A collection that has not answered yet is not

declarations.description:
Three parts: a direction that is up, down or neutral, the metric that moved,
and a label saying over what. The arrow carries the direction and its colour
carries the judgment, and the two are separate properties because they are
separate facts.

**`good` is absent by default, so an unjudged trend is grey.** Every
dashboard convention says up is green, and for churn, latency, error rate,
cost and bounce rate that convention is a lie told in the most legible colour
on the page. A component that guesses is wrong roughly a third of the time
and silent about it; one that waits to be told is uninformative until it is,
which is the cheaper failure. State the metric's polarity once and the
component does the part that varies.

The direction is also written as a word, because a coloured arrow says
nothing to a reader who is not looking at it. `part="direction"` is what the
styled tier clips out of sight and leaves in the accessibility tree.

Both the metric and the label are bare slots. An element whose only job is to
assign itself a slot on connect gives its own host an attribute after
upgrade, which a React consumer's server markup never had.

declarations.description:
**It holds what the player needs and nothing about playing.** A source, a
poster and a name: the entry knows which file it stands for, and the playlist
is what hands that to a player. Nothing here touches a `<video>`, which is
what keeps a playlist usable with a player the consumer configured
themselves.

**A real `<button>`, in a `listitem`.** A playlist is a list of things to
choose, and the list roles are the honest ones: `list` and `listitem` say how
many there are and where you are in them, which `listbox` would too, at the
cost of the pattern a listbox obliges. `Option` records that trap in full,
that a listbox has to keep focus elsewhere and say which item is current with
`aria-activedescendant`. Nothing here needs that, because focus really moves
to the button.

`aria-current` rather than `aria-selected`, which belongs to the roles that
have a selection. What is true of the entry playing now is that it is the one
the player is on.

declarations.description:
The entries again, reachable without leaving the picture. A playlist beside
the player is a list a reader scrolls to; the same list in the control bar is
one they open over the video, which is what a full-screen player has and what
a phone has room for.

**It is placed by the consumer, not rendered by the playlist**, and that is
forced rather than chosen. A shadow root cannot project into a sibling's
light DOM, so nothing the playlist renders can land inside the player's
control bar. What can is an element the consumer writes there, which is what
`Video`'s `controls` slot is for:

```html
<helix-video-playlist>
  <helix-video slot="player" controls>
    <helix-video-playlist-menu slot="controls"></helix-video-playlist-menu>
  </helix-video>
  <helix-video-playlist-item value="one" src="/one.mp4">One</helix-video-playlist-item>
</helix-video-playlist>
```

So it finds its playlist upward rather than being handed one, and that chain
crosses a shadow boundary in the ordinary arrangement, which is why it is
`closestInstance` and not `closest`.

**Choosing dispatches `helix-select`, the same event an entry dispatches.**
It never writes `active` on the playlist, which looks like the shorter path
and would latch the controlled contract: a playlist assigned `active` once
goes quiet and waits for a consumer who was never there. Announcing is what
an entry does, the playlist already listens for it, and a consumer refusing a
selection gets `preventDefault()` on one event rather than two paths that
behave differently.

members.name: watch
members.description:
Watches the playlist for entries arriving, and re-reads it on every open.

Two signals rather than one, because the two facts change on different
clocks and only one of them is observable.

**Which entries exist** is the playlist's light DOM, and a `MutationObserver`
sees it directly.

**Which entry is current** is `active`, a property with no attribute, so
there is nothing to observe: events travel up from the playlist and this
element is below it, and mirroring `active` to a `data-` name is ruled out
on its own merits, `active` being a payload rather than a boolean fact.
Mirroring it was written and reverted here: it put `data-active` onto every
host, which `tree-root.ssr.spec.ts` caught, and the rule it broke was the
one that stops a copied host coming back frozen.

So it is re-read at the moment it is looked at. `helix-open` comes from the
menu in this element's own shadow root, which is the one direction events
do arrive from, and a closed menu showing a stale mark is a thing nobody
can see.

declarations.description:
**The player is slotted, never rendered here.** A consumer's player carries
their appearance, their extra controls, their captions and their poster
treatment, and a playlist that rendered its own would either lose all of that
or grow a property for each of them. `Sandbox` takes its preview and `Menu`
its trigger the same way.

**The entries are markup rather than an array property.** A list of objects
would be the shorter API and it does not survive the trip: React skips every
property it would have to apply imperatively while hydrating, so an array
handed to a custom element is missing on the first paint of every
server-rendered page. `using-the-elements.mdx` carries the measurement. Markup
is also what makes each entry a real button with a real name in it.

**Nothing here plays anything.** It sets `src` on the player and lets the
player be a player. What the playlist owns is which entry is current, and it
moves that on three signals: an entry pressed, `helix-next` or
`helix-previous` from the player, and the player reaching the end.

`ended` advances without asking, because a set of clips that stopped between
each one is a set the reader has to nurse. The clip that follows starts where
the last one left off, which is `autoplay` in the only sense that matters
here: the reader already pressed play once.

All three ways it moves are the reader going somewhere: pressing an entry,
pressing next or previous, or a clip ending and the next one following it.

A press is also what makes the play legal. Autoplay is refused when nothing
the reader did asked for it, so starting here works because this is inside
the gesture that chose the entry, and where it is refused anyway the player
shows its start control and waits.

declarations.description:
**The picture is a real `<video>`.** Decoding, buffering, captions, Picture
in Picture, AirPlay and the codecs a device happens to have are all the
platform's, and none of them can be had from anything else. What is replaced
is the control bar, which is the one part of a video element that cannot be
styled and looks different in every browser.

**Every control is a real control.** The scrubber and the volume are
`<input type="range">`, so a reader gets arrow keys, Home and End, the
platform's own touch target and its screen reader announcement without this
element implementing any of it. Drawing a div and listening for pointer moves
is how a media player ends up unusable from a keyboard.

**Native controls are the fallback, not the default.** Where a consumer sets
`controls`, the browser's bar is used and this one is not drawn: two sets of
controls over one video is worse than either alone, and a consumer who asked
for the native bar has a reason.

The keys are the ones every player uses: Space and `k` to play or pause, the
arrows to seek and to change the volume, `m` to mute, `f` for fullscreen.
They are bound on this element rather than on the document, because a video
is not a palette: keys belong to it only while a reader is on it.

**And none of them where `controls` is set.** The browser's own bar owns
those keys, and two handlers on one press is a video that seeks twice or
plays and immediately pauses. The focus stop goes with them, since the native
controls bring their own.
